MOBILE-001.prerequisites: The target application's APK (Android) or IPA (iOS) file, obtained from the app store or provided by the client. Standard mobile reverse-engineering tools: apktool/jadx for Android, and a jailbroken test device or a static-analysis tool (class-dump, otool) for iOS. A rooted/jailbroken test device or emulator to run the app with debugging attached.
MOBILE-001.whatItIs: The version of the app published to real users still has debug settings turned on — things like Android's 'debuggable' flag left true, verbose logging that shouldn't be there, or hidden test menus reachable through a secret tap pattern. Any of these expose functionality or information that was never meant for regular users.
MOBILE-001.rootCause: Debug settings are genuinely useful during development — attaching a debugger, verbose logs for troubleshooting, test menus for QA. But they need to be explicitly turned off before the app ships. That step either got missed in the release process, or nothing automatically checks for it, so a debug-enabled build made it all the way to the app store.
MOBILE-001.impact: Anyone who can plug into the device — or the user themselves — can attach a debugger and watch or change how the app behaves while it runs. That makes client-side checks like licence validation, root detection and certificate pinning trivial to switch off. On top of that, verbose logging can spill sensitive data into the device log, and leftover test menus can expose an admin panel or an unthrottled API harness that was never meant to be reachable by a real user.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the APK and check the AndroidManifest.xml for `android:debuggable="true"` on the application element, which should never be present in a release build.
For iOS, inspect the app's entitlements (via `codesign -d --entitlements`) for `get-task-allow` set to true, which indicates a debug-signed build rather than a proper distribution/App Store build.

Attempt to attach a debugger (jdb for Android, lldb for iOS on a jailbroken device) to a running instance of the installed app and confirm whether the attach succeeds without any anti-debug countermeasure.
Search decompiled code/strings for test-menu trigger patterns, hidden Intent actions, or verbose logging statements that shouldn't be present in a production build.
Confirm the shipped production build carries the debuggable flag, since a debug build in the store exposes the running app to inspection on any device.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes reverse engineering and debugger-attachment testing against the test installation.
Confirm the debuggable flag/entitlement is present via manifest/entitlement inspection.
Attach a debugger to the running app and set a breakpoint on a security-relevant function (a license or root-detection check) to confirm unhindered runtime inspection/modification is possible.
If a hidden test menu or debug-only functionality is found, trigger it and document exactly what it exposes.
Document the specific debug artifact (manifest flag, entitlement, hidden menu) and its practical exploitability via debugger attachment.

examplePayloads.label: Check AndroidManifest.xml for the debuggable flag
examplePayloads.command: apktool d target_app.apk -o decoded && grep -i 'debuggable' decoded/AndroidManifest.xml

examplePayloads.label: Check iOS app entitlements for debug signing
examplePayloads.command: codesign -d --entitlements :- TargetApp.app | grep -i 'get-task-allow'

examplePayloads.label: Attach a debugger to a running Android app instance
examplePayloads.command: adb shell am start -D -n com.target.app/.MainActivity && jdb -attach localhost:8700

examplePayloads.label: Read the debuggable flag from the installed package
examplePayloads.command: aapt dump badging <app>.apk | grep -i debuggable

variants: Debuggable flag left enabled by default in a build-flavor/CI misconfiguration rather than an intentional development-build leak.
Hidden test/QA menu reachable via a specific tap sequence or ADB Intent broadcast, exposing internal diagnostics rather than debugger-attachment risk specifically.
A release build that is not debuggable itself but ships with a bundled development configuration pointing at test endpoints, which leaks internal infrastructure.
mitigation: Ensure `android:debuggable` is explicitly set to `false` (or omitted, which defaults to false) in the release build variant, and verify this via an automated build-pipeline check rather than manual review alone.
Sign iOS release builds with a proper App Store/Ad Hoc distribution profile that does not include `get-task-allow`, and verify entitlements as a release-gate check.
Strip all test menus, verbose logging, and debug-only code paths from release builds via build-flavor separation (a distinct debug source set never merged into release).
Add automated static analysis (MobSF or an equivalent) to the CI/CD pipeline to catch debug-flag and entitlement misconfigurations before a build reaches the app store.
MOBILE-001.mitigationClientFacing: The version of your app in the store was built in development mode, which leaves it open to inspection and manipulation on any user's device — the equivalent of shipping a product with its service panel unlocked. This makes every other weakness in the app easier for an attacker to find and exploit. The fix is straightforward and belongs in your release process: production builds must have development and debugging features switched off, and that should be checked automatically before a build can be published rather than relied on as a manual step. Confirm the current store build is rebuilt correctly, as the exposure persists until it is replaced.
MOBILE-001.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Debuggable/Test Build in Production” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: anyone who can plug into the device — or the user themselves — can attach a debugger and watch or change how the app behaves while it runs. Poor binary protections make it straightforward to decompile the app and recover hardcoded secrets or bypass client-side checks. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-002.prerequisites: The target application installed on a rooted/jailbroken test device or emulator. A decompiler (jadx for Android, class-dump/Hopper for iOS) to inspect WebView configuration and any JavaScript-bridge interface code. A proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) to intercept and modify content loaded into the WebView.
MOBILE-002.whatItIs: The app uses a WebView (an embedded browser) to show web content, but sets it up insecurely — turning on JavaScript along with a bridge that lets loaded web content call sensitive native app functions, allowing it to load any file on the device, or loading content over plain HTTP instead of HTTPS. If an attacker can control what content gets loaded (by intercepting traffic, compromising an ad network, or a malicious link), they can run code with access to whatever that native bridge exposes.
MOBILE-002.rootCause: A WebView is powerful and general-purpose, and setting it up securely means getting several easy-to-miss settings right — limiting the JavaScript bridge to fully trusted sources, blocking universal file access, forcing HTTPS-only content. When a bridge gets added for a legitimate reason (letting web content call native app code) without also locking down which content is allowed to use it, anything the WebView loads — including something an attacker controls — inherits that bridge's power.
MOBILE-002.impact: If an attacker can get the WebView to load content they control, they can call the app's exposed native functions directly from that page. They might reach it by intercepting an insecurely-loaded page, forcing a malicious redirect, or abusing a separate injection flaw elsewhere in the app. What that gets them depends entirely on what the bridge exposes — commonly reading local files, reaching device sensors or contacts, or triggering native functionality the page should never have been able to touch.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and locate all WebView instantiations, checking their configuration for `setJavaScriptEnabled(true)` combined with `addJavascriptInterface()` (Android) or an equivalent `WKScriptMessageHandler`/`window.webkit.messageHandlers` bridge (iOS).
For each JavaScript bridge found, review what native methods/classes it exposes and assess whether any allow file access, sensitive data retrieval, or arbitrary code execution.

Check whether the WebView restricts content loading to a specific, trusted origin (via `shouldOverrideUrlLoading`/`WKNavigationDelegate` origin checks) or loads any URL it's given, including ones reachable via a deep link or a MITM-redirected request.

Test whether the WebView has universal file-access enabled (`setAllowFileAccessFromFileURLs`/`setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs` on Android) which would allow a loaded local HTML file to read other local files via `file://` URLs.
Establish whether the in-app browser component is configured to run local code and read local files, since that combination lets loaded content reach the device.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes MITM/content-injection testing against the test installation's WebView.
Identify a WebView loading content over an insecurely-verified channel (HTTP, or HTTPS without certificate pinning) and position a proxy to intercept and modify that content.
Inject JavaScript into the intercepted page content that invokes the exposed native bridge method(s) identified during discovery.
Confirm the injected JavaScript successfully triggers the native functionality (e.g. retrieves a piece of device data, reads a local file) as proof of concept.
Document the exact bridge method(s) exploited, the content-loading weakness that allowed injection, and the resulting native-functionality access achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Search decompiled code for insecure WebView/JS-bridge configuration
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk && grep -rn 'addJavascriptInterface\|setJavaScriptEnabled' decompiled_output/

examplePayloads.label: Intercept and inject JavaScript into WebView-loaded content via proxy
examplePayloads.command: # Burp: intercept the WebView's HTTP(S) response, inject <script>Android.exposedMethod('poc')</script> into the response body

examplePayloads.label: Test universal file access via a crafted local HTML page
examplePayloads.command: echo '<script>fetch("file:///data/data/com.target.app/shared_prefs/config.xml").then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>Android.exfil(t))</script>' > poc.html

examplePayloads.label: Locate the in-app browser configuration and flag script/file access in the decompiled source
examplePayloads.command: grep -rniE 'setJavaScriptEnabled|allowFileAccess|addJavascriptInterface' <decompiled-src>/

variants: JavaScript bridge exposed to any origin versus one that attempts an origin check but is bypassable (e.g. checking only a substring of the URL rather than the full, validated origin).
Universal file-access enabled, allowing a loaded local or attacker-supplied HTML file to read arbitrary local files via `file://` URLs independent of any JavaScript-bridge exposure.
A browser component that loads remote content over an unauthenticated channel, so a network attacker supplies the page the component then trusts with local access.
mitigation: Restrict any JavaScript bridge to load only from a specific, HTTPS-enforced, certificate-pinned origin, verified via a strict `shouldOverrideUrlLoading`/navigation-delegate check rather than a substring match.
Disable universal file access and universal access from file URLs unless there is a specific, well-understood need, and never combine either with an exposed JavaScript bridge.
Expose only the minimal set of native methods genuinely required through the bridge, and validate/sanitize all parameters passed from JavaScript before acting on them natively.
Where feasible, avoid WebView-based hybrid architectures for security-sensitive functionality entirely, preferring native UI for anything touching sensitive data or device capabilities.
MOBILE-002.mitigationClientFacing: Your app displays web content inside itself, and that built-in browser is configured permissively enough that the content it shows can reach into the device — running code and reading local files. If any of that content can be influenced by an attacker, so can the device. The fix is to lock the built-in browser down so displayed content can only display, not call into the app or the device, and to ensure it only ever loads content over a verified, encrypted connection. This is an important item because it turns an ordinary web weakness into a route onto the user's phone.
MOBILE-002.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Insecure WebView Configuration” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: if an attacker can get the WebView to load content they control, they can call the app's exposed native functions directly from that page. Insufficient input/output validation is the mobile equivalent of the injection classes that dominate web breaches. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-003.prerequisites: The target application installed on a rooted/jailbroken test device or emulator with Frida available for runtime instrumentation. A decompiler to locate the biometric-authentication call site and understand how its result is checked.
MOBILE-003.whatItIs: The app uses fingerprint or face unlock to protect something sensitive (opening the app, approving a payment), but it decides whether that worked just by checking a simple true/false result in its own code, instead of using the successful unlock to release an actual cryptographic key that only a genuine, real authentication could unlock. That true/false check can be forced to 'true' using standard runtime tampering tools, completely bypassing the biometric check without ever actually scanning a real fingerprint or face.
MOBILE-003.rootCause: The phone's biometric system itself is genuinely tamper-resistant at the hardware level. But if the app only uses it as a simple yes/no flag in its own logic ('unlock succeeded, so set this flag to true and continue'), instead of tying that unlock to actually releasing a protected key from secure hardware, the real security boundary is just an ordinary function call inside the app — something that can be intercepted and manipulated.
MOBILE-003.impact: An attacker who can run code on the device — through a rooted or jailbroken phone, or malware with enough privilege — can force the app's 'authentication succeeded' result to fire whether or not any real check happened. The biometric gate is then completely bypassed, along with whatever it was protecting. They do not need a fake fingerprint, because the prompt itself is never shown: the result is simply overwritten after the fact.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the app and locate the biometric-authentication call site, checking whether the success callback merely sets a boolean flag consumed elsewhere in application logic, or is used to unwrap/decrypt a cryptographic key tied to the Keystore/Secure Enclave.
Attach Frida to a running instance and enumerate the class/method implementing the biometric callback interface to confirm it's hookable.
With authorization, hook the identified success-callback method to force it to report success, then attempt to proceed past the biometric prompt without providing genuine biometric input.

Where the app does bind to a Keystore/Secure Enclave key, separately verify that the key's access policy genuinely requires biometric authentication for use (`setUserAuthenticationRequired` correctly configured) rather than being retrievable through some other, unguarded code path.
Determine whether the local authentication decision is enforced by the operating system's secure hardware or merely returned to app code that can be patched.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes runtime instrumentation of the test installation's biometric-authentication flow.
Attach Frida to the running app and hook the biometric-authentication success-callback method identified during discovery.
Trigger the app's biometric prompt, then use the hook to force a success result regardless of what (if anything) is presented to the actual biometric sensor.
Confirm the app proceeds to the protected functionality despite no genuine biometric verification having occurred.
Document the exact hooked method, the bypass technique, and whether the underlying sensitive operation (a Keystore-protected key) was also actually bypassed, or only the app's own boolean gate.

examplePayloads.label: Decompile to locate the biometric callback implementation
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk && grep -rn 'onAuthenticationSucceeded\|BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationCallback' decompiled_output/

examplePayloads.label: Frida hook forcing the biometric success callback
examplePayloads.command: frida -U -n com.target.app -l force_biometric_success.js  # Interceptor.attach(onAuthenticationSucceeded address/method, { onEnter: () => { /* force proceed */ } })

examplePayloads.label: Generic objection-based biometric bypass (Android)
examplePayloads.command:
objection -g com.target.app explore
android biometric bypass

examplePayloads.label: Confirm at runtime whether the authentication result is a patchable in-app check
examplePayloads.command: # attach an instrumentation toolkit and observe whether the auth callback result can be overridden

variants: Biometric gate bypassed via hooking the boolean callback only, versus a deeper bypass that also compromises an improperly-configured Keystore key lacking a genuine `setUserAuthenticationRequired` binding.
iOS equivalent using LocalAuthentication's `evaluatePolicy` completion handler hooked via Frida rather than bound to Keychain item access control.
Local authentication that gates the interface but not the data, so the protected content is readable directly from storage without passing the check at all.
mitigation: Bind biometric authentication to a cryptographic operation — use the result of successful authentication to unwrap or use a key stored in the Android Keystore (with `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)`) or iOS Keychain/Secure Enclave (with an appropriate access-control flag), rather than relying on a boolean application-logic flag.

Ensure the protected sensitive operation (decrypting data, authorizing a transaction) is only possible using the key released by genuine biometric authentication, so that hooking the app's own callback provides no path to the actual protected resource.
Apply root/jailbreak detection and integrity checks as defense-in-depth, understanding they raise the bar for instrumentation-based attacks but don't eliminate them on a determined attacker's device.
Avoid treating client-side biometric gates as a substitute for server-side authorization checks on any sensitive action initiated after the gate.
MOBILE-003.mitigationClientFacing: The check that unlocks your app with a fingerprint, face or local PIN can be bypassed, because the decision is made in a place an attacker with the device can reach and override rather than being enforced by the phone's secure hardware. The fix is to have that hardware make and hold the decision, and — just as importantly — to ensure the protected data is genuinely locked rather than merely hidden behind the unlock screen, so it cannot be read directly from storage. This matters most for lost or stolen devices, which is precisely the scenario the lock is there for.
MOBILE-003.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Weak Local Authentication / Biometric Bypass” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: an attacker who can run code on the device — through a rooted or jailbroken phone, or malware with enough privilege — can force the app's 'authentication succeeded' result to fire whether or not any real check happened. Insecure authentication/authorization on mobile lets a tampered client bypass checks the server should have enforced. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-004.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device, with a test account. A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) to capture and replay session tokens, and the ability to control device/network state to simulate a lost/stolen-device or extended-idle scenario.
MOBILE-004.whatItIs: The app's login session stays valid forever, or for an unreasonably long time, with no expiration, no timeout after inactivity, and no real way to revoke it. Once issued, the same session keeps working for every future request, no matter how much time has passed, whether the user logged out on another device, or whether the phone itself was reported lost or stolen.
MOBILE-004.rootCause: Session length and revocation were built around convenience — not making users log in repeatedly — without the server actually enforcing a maximum lifetime, an inactivity timeout, or a real revocation check on every request. The token's validity depends only on whether it was ever issued, not on whether the session is actually still legitimate right now.
MOBILE-004.impact: A stolen token stays usable indefinitely, or at least far longer than a properly-bounded session should allow. It could have been captured through device theft, intercepted network traffic, or extracted from a backup. Worse, a user who deliberately logs out on one device may reasonably believe they have ended their session, while a captured copy of that same token continues to work.
stepsToIdentify: Capture a valid session token during normal app use via a proxy, then attempt to reuse it after progressively longer periods of app inactivity to determine whether any idle-timeout enforcement exists server-side.

Perform an explicit "log out" action within the app, then attempt to replay the previously-captured token directly against the backend API (bypassing the app UI) to check whether the server actually invalidates it, or whether logout is purely a client-side state change.
Check whether the token has a JWT-style expiration claim (`exp`) and, if so, whether the server actually enforces it or merely issues it as informational metadata the client happens to respect.

Determine whether any "log out of all devices"/session-management feature exists in the app, and if so, confirm it actually invalidates previously-issued tokens server-side rather than only affecting the current session's local state.
Establish whether the session token is invalidated on the server at logout or merely discarded by the app, since a server-live token remains usable if captured.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes session-token capture and replay testing against the test installation using a test account.
Capture a valid session token via the proxy during normal app use.
Perform an explicit logout within the app, then replay the captured token directly against the backend API and confirm whether it's still accepted.
If accepted, wait a representative extended period (or simulate device-loss conditions) and replay again to further characterize the token's effective, unbounded lifetime.
Document the exact token type, its claimed vs. actual expiration behavior, and whether logout provides genuine server-side revocation.

examplePayloads.label: Decode a JWT token to inspect its claimed expiration
examplePayloads.command: echo '<captured-jwt>' | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d | jq .

examplePayloads.command: # replay a captured session token against an authenticated endpoint after logging out in the app

variants: Token technically has a short `exp` claim, but the server doesn't actually validate it, accepting expired tokens indefinitely regardless of the claim's value.
Refresh-token mechanism itself never expires or is never invalidated on logout, allowing an attacker to mint fresh access tokens indefinitely even if the access token itself has a short lifetime.
A session that survives a credential change on another device, so a stolen token outlives the password reset intended to revoke it.
mitigation: Enforce both an absolute maximum token lifetime and an idle-timeout period server-side, independent of any client-side expiration claim the token itself carries.

Implement genuine server-side session/token revocation (a token blocklist or a short-lived-token-plus-refresh-token model with revocable refresh tokens) so that logout actually invalidates the token rather than only clearing local client state.
Provide a "log out of all devices"/active-session-management feature that genuinely revokes all previously-issued tokens for the account, for use after a suspected device loss or compromise.
Validate token expiration server-side on every request rather than trusting the client to respect a claimed expiration value.
MOBILE-004.mitigationClientFacing: When a user logs out of your app, or changes their password, the session is not reliably ended on your servers — only forgotten by the app. That means a session token captured earlier keeps working, so logging out does not actually revoke access and a password change does not lock out a thief. The fix is for the server to invalidate the session on logout and on any credential change, so that ending a session on the app ends it everywhere. This is a server-side correction and it matters because users reasonably assume that logging out protects them.
MOBILE-004.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Improper Session Handling” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: a stolen token stays usable indefinitely, or at least far longer than a properly-bounded session should allow. Insecure authentication/authorization on mobile lets a tampered client bypass checks the server should have enforced. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-005.prerequisites: The target application installed on a rooted/jailbroken test device with Frida available. A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) with its CA certificate available, and a certificate-pinning-bypass script set (objection's built-in bypass, or a curated public bypass-script collection) appropriate to the app's pinning implementation.
MOBILE-005.whatItIs: The app does implement certificate pinning, checking that it is really talking to the genuine server. But the way it is built lets standard, publicly available bypass tools defeat it anyway. Perhaps it is only enforced in some parts of the app and not others. Perhaps the check itself is a simple comparison that is easy to intercept. Or the app uses a popular library's pinning feature in a way that public bypass scripts already target specifically.
MOBILE-005.rootCause: Pinning was added, but without extra protection making it resistant to runtime tampering tools (like Frida) — no obfuscation of the check itself, no anti-hooking measures, no redundant checks. A pinning check that's technically present but easily bypassed gives a false sense of security if it's never actually tested against the tools that would defeat it.
MOBILE-005.impact: An attacker who neutralises the pinning check ends up with exactly the same full interception capability as if pinning had never been implemented at all. The practical benefit of having built it is therefore close to zero against anyone who knows the standard bypass tooling and can run it on a rooted or jailbroken device. It stops a casual observer and nobody else.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the app does implement some form of certificate pinning (via decompilation, looking for a pin-comparison or a well-known pinning library's initialization) as distinct from the missing-pinning finding.

Attach Frida with a standard, publicly-available universal SSL-pinning-bypass script (objection's `android sslpinning disable`, or an equivalent iOS script) and attempt to intercept the app's HTTPS traffic through a proxy while the bypass is active.
If the standard bypass succeeds without modification, this confirms the pinning implementation is defeatable by widely-available tooling rather than requiring bespoke reverse engineering.

Check whether pinning is enforced consistently across every network call the app makes, or only on some endpoints (a common partial-implementation gap even when the core pinning mechanism itself is reasonably robust).
Confirm whether the pinning implementation validates the full trust chain or only a leaf property that a substituted certificate can also satisfy.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes runtime instrumentation and MITM proxy testing against the test installation's pinned network traffic.
Set up the intercepting proxy with its CA certificate installed on the test device's trust store.
Attach Frida with the appropriate universal SSL-pinning-bypass script for the platform and networking library in use.
Attempt a normal, sensitive network action (login, an API call) within the app and confirm the proxy successfully captures the decrypted traffic despite the app's pinning implementation being active.
Document which specific bypass script/technique succeeded and note any endpoints where pinning enforcement appeared inconsistent.

variants: Pinning implemented via a third-party networking library (OkHttp CertificatePinner, TrustKit) with a known, publicly-documented bypass technique specific to that library's implementation pattern.
Pinning enforced on the primary API traffic but absent on a secondary channel (analytics/crash-reporting SDK traffic) within the same app.
Pinning enforced on the primary API but omitted on analytics or update channels, which become the interception point instead.
mitigation: Combine certificate pinning with anti-hooking/anti-Frida detection and code obfuscation specifically hardening the pin-validation code path, understanding this raises the bar rather than providing an absolute guarantee against a sufficiently determined attacker.
Implement multiple, independent pinning checks at different layers (network library level and an additional application-level check) so defeating one doesn't automatically defeat the other.
Ensure pinning is applied consistently across every network-communicating component of the app, including analytics/crash-reporting/third-party SDKs, not just the primary API client.
Periodically re-test pinning robustness against current, publicly-available bypass tooling as part of routine mobile security assessments, since bypass techniques and tooling evolve.
MOBILE-005.mitigationClientFacing: Your app tries to verify it is talking to your genuine servers, but the check is implemented weakly enough to be defeated, which lets an attacker on the same network read and alter the app's traffic. The fix is to implement that verification correctly — validating the full chain of trust rather than a single property a fake can copy — and to apply it to every connection the app makes, including the analytics and update channels that are commonly left unprotected and become the way in. This protects users on untrusted networks such as public Wi-Fi, where this kind of interception is easiest.
MOBILE-005.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Certificate Pinning Bypass” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: an attacker who neutralises the pinning check ends up with exactly the same full interception capability as if pinning had never been implemented at all. Insecure communication — cleartext or unpinned TLS — lets anyone on the same network read or alter the app's traffic. It is worth confirming and fixing early, before it is chained into something larger.

MOBILE-006.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device connected to a network you control. A packet-capture tool (Wireshark/tcpdump) or a transparent network proxy positioned to observe all of the app's network traffic, independent of whether the app attempts certificate pinning (since this finding covers traffic sent without TLS at all, not a pinning bypass).
MOBILE-006.whatItIs: The app sends data over plain, unencrypted HTTP for at least one of its network features. The main API is often fine, while an analytics service, an update check, or a third-party ad SDK is not. The standard to aim for is HTTPS for absolutely everything the app talks to over the network.
MOBILE-006.rootCause: Not every part of the app that talks over the network got the same 'always use HTTPS' treatment. This usually happens because a secondary feature — analytics, ads, an update check — was added by a different team or a third-party SDK, and it never went through the same security review that covered the main API traffic.
MOBILE-006.impact: Anyone watching the network path can read the traffic directly — a malicious or compromised Wi-Fi access point, or an attacker positioned on a shared network. Where that traffic carries login credentials, session tokens or personal data, it becomes credential theft or session hijacking. And because unencrypted traffic has no tamper protection either, an attacker can actively modify it, for example injecting a malicious response to the app's update check.
stepsToIdentify: Capture the app's full network traffic during a comprehensive walkthrough of every feature (login, primary functionality, settings, and any background/update-check activity) using Wireshark or a transparent proxy configured to capture all traffic, not just HTTP(S).

Filter the capture for any traffic on standard unencrypted ports/protocols (HTTP on port 80, or a custom unencrypted protocol) rather than assuming all traffic is HTTPS based on the app's primary, most visible functionality.
For each unencrypted channel found, identify what data it carries and flag any credential, token, or sensitive user data specifically.

Check the app's manifest/configuration for Android Network Security Config or iOS App Transport Security (ATS) settings, since an overly permissive exception (`cleartextTrafficPermitted="true"` or an ATS exception domain) is frequently the specific configuration enabling this finding.
Confirm whether any endpoint falls back to cleartext, testing each host the app contacts rather than assuming the main API represents them all.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes network traffic capture during a full feature walkthrough of the test installation.
Capture traffic across every feature of the app, including background/secondary channels not immediately visible in the primary UI flow.
Identify and extract any sensitive data observed in cleartext.
Where credentials/tokens are captured, attempt to use them against the corresponding service as proof-of-impact evidence, using only test accounts.
Document every unencrypted channel found, the data it exposed, and the specific Network Security Config/ATS configuration responsible for permitting it.

variants: Primary API correctly using HTTPS while a bundled third-party SDK (ads, analytics) communicates over plain HTTP independently.
Network Security Config/ATS correctly restrictive by default, but with a broad domain-wildcard exception that inadvertently covers more traffic than intended.
A primary API over encrypted transport while an image, analytics or config host is fetched in cleartext, disclosing usage and enabling content tampering.
mitigation: Enforce HTTPS for every network-communicating feature of the app, including third-party SDK traffic, with no cleartext exception unless a specific, narrowly-scoped, documented business need exists.

Set Android's Network Security Config to disallow cleartext traffic by default (`cleartextTrafficPermitted="false"`) at the base-config level, adding only narrowly-scoped, justified exceptions where unavoidable.
Enable and avoid broadly exempting iOS App Transport Security (ATS), reviewing any exception domain list for necessity.
Audit third-party SDKs specifically for their network-security posture before integration, since these are a common source of overlooked cleartext traffic.
MOBILE-006.mitigationClientFacing: Some of your app's network traffic is unencrypted, so data — potentially including credentials and personal information — travels in a form anyone on the same network can read. Often the main connection is protected while a secondary one for images, analytics or configuration is not, and that overlooked channel both leaks data and lets an attacker alter what the app receives. The fix is to encrypt every connection the app makes and verify each destination, testing them individually rather than assuming the main one represents them all. This is a direct exposure of data in transit and matters most on public networks.
MOBILE-006.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Insecure Network Communication” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: anyone watching the network path can read the traffic directly — a malicious or compromised Wi-Fi access point, or an attacker positioned on a shared network. Insecure communication — cleartext or unpinned TLS — lets anyone on the same network read or alter the app's traffic. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-007.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA for decompilation. A decompiler (jadx for Android, Hopper/class-dump for iOS) to locate random-value-generation call sites, and a scripting environment to statistically test generated output for predictability if source access allows extraction of the generation routine.
MOBILE-007.whatItIs: The app generates a value that needs to be genuinely unpredictable — a session token, a password-reset code, an encryption value — using an ordinary random-number function (like Math.random()) instead of one specifically designed to be cryptographically secure. Or it uses the right kind of secure generator, but starts it off with a predictable seed (like the current time), which narrows down how unpredictable the output really is.
MOBILE-007.rootCause: Regular random functions are simpler to use and perfectly fine for things like animations or test data — but they're not built to resist someone trying to guess the output. It's easy to overlook the difference between 'random enough for everyday use' and 'genuinely unpredictable enough to be secure' when a developer just grabs the first random function that comes to mind instead of deliberately picking the secure one for something sensitive.
MOBILE-007.impact: Where the predictable value protects something important — a password-reset token, a session ID, or an encryption starting value — an attacker who works out the generator's pattern can predict values it has produced or will produce next. For common non-secure random functions this is straightforward, since the internal state can often be reconstructed from just a handful of observed outputs. That allows forged reset tokens, hijacked sessions, or broken encryption that depended on those values being unguessable.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and search for random-value generation call sites, flagging any use of `java.util.Random`, `Math.random()`, or C's `rand()`/`srand()` in a context that produces a security-sensitive value (tokens, IVs, nonces).

For each flagged call site, trace how the generated value is seeded — an explicit, predictable seed (current time, a device ID) is a more severe variant even if the underlying algorithm were otherwise acceptable.

Where the app communicates with a backend, capture multiple instances of the security-sensitive value (e.g. successive password-reset tokens for test accounts) and statistically analyze them for a discernible, non-random pattern.

Confirm whether a proper CSPRNG (`SecureRandom`, `SecRandomCopyBytes`) is available and used elsewhere in the same app for other purposes, indicating the specific flagged use is an inconsistency rather than a codebase-wide gap.
Establish whether security-relevant values — tokens, nonces, identifiers — are drawn from a cryptographically secure source rather than a predictable one.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes reverse-engineering and predictability-testing of the identified random-value generation routine.
Extract or replicate the exact non-cryptographic generation algorithm and seeding logic identified via decompilation.
Collect a representative sample of generated values (e.g. successive test-account password-reset tokens) via authorized test requests.

Attempt to reconstruct the generator's internal state from the collected sample and predict a subsequent value, then confirm the prediction is accepted as valid by the backend (e.g. successfully using a predicted reset token).
Document the exact generation routine, seeding weakness, and the demonstrated predictability/forgery achieved.

examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk && grep -rn 'java.util.Random\|Math.random' decompiled_output/ | grep -iE 'token|nonce|reset|session'

examplePayloads.label: Collect a sample of generated tokens for pattern analysis (authorized test accounts)
examplePayloads.command: for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -X POST https://<api-endpoint>/password-reset -d '{"email":"test'$i'@example.test"}'; done

examplePayloads.label: Statistically test collected values for predictability
examplePayloads.command: python3 analyze_token_entropy.py collected_tokens.txt

examplePayloads.label: Locate random-number usage in the decompiled source and flag insecure generators
examplePayloads.command: grep -rniE 'Math.random|java.util.Random|arc4random\(' <decompiled-src>/

variants: A cryptographically-appropriate PRNG used but seeded with a predictable value (timestamp, device ID) rather than a properly-sourced random seed, which weakens an otherwise-correct algorithm choice.

Non-cryptographic randomness used specifically for an encryption IV/nonce, breaking the uniqueness/unpredictability guarantee the encryption scheme depends on even if the encryption algorithm itself (e.g. AES) is otherwise correctly implemented.
A secure generator seeded from a predictable value such as time, which reintroduces predictability despite the correct algorithm.
mitigation: Use a cryptographically secure random number generator (`SecureRandom` on Android/Java, `SecRandomCopyBytes` on iOS, or the platform-equivalent CSPRNG) for every security-sensitive value: tokens, nonces, IVs, and password-reset codes.
Never seed a CSPRNG with a predictable value; rely on the platform's own properly-sourced entropy for seeding.

Audit the codebase for all random-value generation call sites as part of a security-focused code review, distinguishing security-sensitive uses (requiring a CSPRNG) from general-purpose ones (where a standard PRNG remains acceptable).

Where server-side generation is feasible for a given value (e.g. password-reset tokens), prefer generating it server-side using the server platform's CSPRNG rather than relying on client-side generation at all.
MOBILE-007.mitigationClientFacing: Your app generates security-sensitive values — such as tokens — using a method that is predictable rather than truly random, which means an attacker can anticipate them and, for example, forge a password-reset link or a session. Randomness is the foundation these protections rest on, and a predictable source quietly removes it while everything appears to work. The fix is to draw all security-sensitive values from the platform's proper cryptographic random source and to ensure it is not seeded from anything guessable. This is a contained code change, but its consequences reach whatever those values protect, so it warrants prompt attention.
MOBILE-007.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Insecure Random Number Generation” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: where the predictable value protects something important — a password-reset token, a session ID, or an encryption starting value — an attacker who works out the generator's pattern can predict values it has produced or will produce next. Weak cryptography on mobile turns encrypted-at-rest data back into plaintext for anyone who extracts it. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-008.prerequisites: At least two separate installations of the target application (on two different test devices, or two separate app-data resets on the same device) for comparison. A decompiler to locate the key-generation/retrieval logic, and a means to extract the actual key material from each installation for comparison.
MOBILE-008.whatItIs: The app uses the same encryption key on every device it is installed on. That happens either because the key is hardcoded directly into the app, or because the code generating it always produces the same result regardless of device. The safe alternative is generating and securely storing a unique key for each individual installation.
MOBILE-008.rootCause: Generating a genuinely unique key per device and storing it securely takes deliberate extra work — using the phone's secure key storage to create and hold a key tied specifically to that device. Just embedding one shared key directly in the app is much simpler, but it means anyone who extracts that key from any single copy of the app (which requires no special access to any particular victim's phone) gets a key that works for every other installation too.
MOBILE-008.impact: An attacker only has to extract the key once, from any copy of the app they download themselves. They never need access to a specific victim's phone. That single key then decrypts the protected data on every other user's device, turning what should have been one device's compromise into a compromise affecting the entire user base.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and locate the cryptographic key-generation or key-retrieval logic used for locally-encrypted data.

Determine whether the key is a literal, hardcoded value in the binary, or is generated/derived using any per-installation or per-device-specific input (a securely-generated random value stored in platform secure storage, or a value derived from device-specific hardware identifiers).
Install the app on two separate devices (or reset and reinstall on the same device) and extract the key material from each installation using the identified generation/retrieval logic.
Compare the extracted key values directly — identical values across independent installations confirm the shared-key finding.
Confirm whether the cryptographic key is unique per installation or shared across all installs, since a shared key compromises every user's data at once.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes key extraction and comparison across multiple test installations.
Extract the key material from a first test installation using the method identified via decompilation.
Extract the key material from a second, independent test installation using the same method.
Confirm the two extracted keys are identical, proving the key is shared rather than uniquely generated per installation.
Demonstrate impact by using the extracted key from one installation to decrypt locally-protected data from the other installation, confirming cross-installation decryption succeeds.

examplePayloads.command: frida -U -n com.target.app -l dump_crypto_key.js

examplePayloads.command: python3 -c "from Crypto.Cipher import AES; ..."  # decrypt install-B's local data file using install-A's extracted key

examplePayloads.command: # trace the key-derivation call at runtime and confirm whether it incorporates per-device material

variants: Key hardcoded directly in the binary versus derived deterministically at runtime from a static, non-device-specific constant, which is functionally equivalent in impact despite appearing more sophisticated.

Key correctly generated with per-installation randomness at first launch, but then unintentionally restored to a prior, now-shared value via an insecure backup/restore mechanism (overlaps with the sensitive-data-in-backups finding).
A per-install key that is nonetheless backed up and restored to a new device, extending its lifetime and exposure beyond the original install.
mitigation: Generate a genuinely unique, cryptographically random key per installation at first launch, using the platform's CSPRNG, and store it exclusively in the platform's secure key storage (Android Keystore, iOS Keychain/Secure Enclave) rather than embedding it in the binary.
Never derive a data-protection key from a static, app-wide constant; ensure any derivation input includes genuine per-installation entropy.

Exclude the securely-stored key from any backup mechanism (or ensure the backup itself is encrypted with a separate, user-specific credential) so a restored backup doesn't inadvertently propagate a shared key.
Audit key-management code specifically for this pattern during any cryptography-focused code review, since it's easy to overlook when the encryption algorithm choice itself is otherwise sound.
MOBILE-008.mitigationClientFacing: Your app protects data on the device with an encryption key that is the same for every installation rather than unique to each user, which means recovering the key once — from any copy of the app — exposes the protected data for all users. The fix is to derive a unique key per installation, tied to the device's secure storage, so that compromising one user's data does not compromise everyone's. Because a shared key affects the whole user base at once, this is a higher priority than its technical description might suggest, and any data protected by the shared key should be treated as exposed.
MOBILE-008.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Insecure Reuse of Cryptographic Key Across App Instances” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: an attacker only has to extract the key once, from any copy of the app they download themselves. Improper credential and platform usage is a routine mobile finding, where secrets or permissions handled wrongly expose the user. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-009.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device. A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) with its CA certificate installed into the device's trust store, and a means to route the app's traffic through the proxy (system proxy settings, or a VPN-based traffic-capture app).
MOBILE-009.whatItIs: The app talks to its server over HTTPS but does no certificate pinning at all — it just relies entirely on the phone's built-in list of trusted certificate authorities. That means any certificate the phone trusts (which anyone can get for a domain they own, or one added by installing a rogue certificate) is enough for someone to sit in the middle of that 'secure' connection.
MOBILE-009.rootCause: Certificate pinning was never added, probably because it adds ongoing work — coordinating pin updates whenever the certificate gets renewed, and handling pin failures gracefully so a routine cert renewal doesn't break the app for everyone. That extra effort got deprioritized in favor of just shipping without it.
MOBILE-009.impact: An attacker on the network path can silently read and modify everything between the app and its backend, including login credentials, session tokens and business data. They might be running a rogue Wi-Fi access point, sitting on a compromised local network, or relying on a malicious certificate installed on the device. The app displays no warning, so the user has no signal that anything is wrong.
stepsToIdentify: Install the testing proxy's CA certificate into the test device's trust store (a straightforward, unprivileged action on most test devices/emulators) and configure the app's traffic to route through the proxy.
Launch the app and exercise any network-dependent feature (login, data sync, an API call) while observing whether the proxy successfully decrypts the traffic.
If traffic is fully visible in the proxy without any connection failure or app-level warning, certificate pinning is confirmed absent.
Cross-reference against the certificate-pinning-bypass-specific finding to distinguish this (no pinning at all) from a case where pinning is present but defeatable.
Confirm pinning is genuinely absent by substituting a trusted certificate, rather than inferring its presence from the configuration alone.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes MITM proxy testing against the test installation's network traffic.
Install the proxy's CA certificate into the test device's trust store and route the app's traffic through the intercepting proxy.
Perform a normal, sensitive action within the app (login, an API call involving test data) and confirm the proxy captures the decrypted content.
Document the specific sensitive data observed in the intercepted traffic as impact evidence.

Note whether the interception succeeded with no special effort beyond standard proxy/CA setup, distinguishing this finding's low-effort exploitability from a scenario requiring an active pinning bypass.

variants: No pinning at all across every network call the app makes, versus pinning present on the primary API but absent on a secondary channel (analytics, ads, update-check) — the latter overlaps with the weak-pinning-implementation finding's partial-coverage variant.

Pinning implemented only on the primary API domain while a secondary domain (analytics SDK, ad network, in-app update service) remains unpinned, giving an attacker a softer target to intercept sensitive tokens that get replayed across domains.
Pinning present in the app's own code but bypassed by a bundled component that makes its own unpinned connections.
mitigation: Implement certificate or public-key pinning for all backend connections, validating against a pinned value embedded in the app rather than relying solely on OS trust-store validation.
Pin the public key (SPKI hash) where possible rather than the full certificate, so certificate renewal doesn't require an app update as long as the key is reused.
Implement a pin-rotation/backup-pin strategy to avoid bricking the app on a legitimate certificate change, and monitor for pin-validation failures in production as a potential MITM indicator.
Apply pinning consistently across every network endpoint the app communicates with, not just the primary authentication/API channel.
MOBILE-009.mitigationClientFacing: Your app does not firmly verify it is talking to your genuine servers, so an attacker positioned on the network can insert themselves in the middle and read or alter the app's traffic, including credentials. The protection — certificate pinning — tells the app exactly which server identity to accept and refuse everything else. It needs to cover every connection the app makes, not only the main one, since update and analytics channels are frequently left unprotected and become the interception point. This is most exploitable on untrusted networks, and closing it materially raises the effort required to intercept your users' data.
MOBILE-009.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Missing Certificate Pinning” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: an attacker on the network path can silently read and modify everything between the app and its backend, including login credentials, session tokens and business data. Insecure communication — cleartext or unpinned TLS — lets anyone on the same network read or alter the app's traffic. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-010.prerequisites: The target application installed on a rooted/jailbroken test device (or an emulator with root access) sufficient to access the app's private data directory directly. File-system search/inspection tools, and a decompiler if the storage appears encoded rather than cleartext.
MOBILE-010.whatItIs: The app stores sensitive data — cached credentials, session tokens, personal user info, business data — in plain, readable form inside its own private storage area (like a local database or settings file), instead of encrypting it with a properly managed, device-secured key.
MOBILE-010.rootCause: This private storage area was treated as automatically safe, on the assumption that the phone's normal app sandboxing (which does stop other apps from reading it) is protection enough. That doesn't account for a rooted or jailbroken phone, a full device backup being extracted, or someone physically accessing a lost or stolen phone — all of which get around that sandbox entirely and expose whatever is stored there in plain text.
MOBILE-010.impact: Anyone with root or jailbreak access, an unencrypted device backup, or physical access plus forensic tools can read the data directly. They never touch the app's login or permission checks, because the data is sitting readable on disk. That turns a single lost or compromised device into full data exposure, no matter how well the app's network-facing security was built.
stepsToIdentify: Use the application normally to generate representative sensitive data (log in, perform typical actions) then access the device's private app-data directory directly (via root/jailbreak access, or `adb shell run-as` for a debuggable Android app).
Inspect SharedPreferences/UserDefaults XML/plist files, local SQLite databases, and any flat files in the app's private directory for plaintext sensitive content.
For content that appears encoded rather than cleartext, attempt straightforward decoding (Base64, simple XOR) before concluding genuine encryption is in use.

Check whether the platform's proper secure-storage facility (Android Keystore-backed EncryptedSharedPreferences, iOS Keychain) is used for genuinely sensitive fields specifically, or whether everything is stored in ordinary, unencrypted app-private storage.
Establish what protects the locally-stored data — encryption, sandbox permissions, or neither — since each fails to a different level of device access.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes local file-system inspection of the test installation's private data storage.
Generate representative sensitive data through normal app use.
Access the app's private data directory using root/jailbreak access (or `adb shell run-as <package>` for a debuggable build) and extract the relevant storage files.
Confirm the data is readable in plaintext (or trivially decodable) without needing the app's own credentials or any additional secret.
Document the exact storage location, the type of sensitive data found, and the storage format (plaintext, weakly encoded, or genuinely but improperly encrypted).

variants: Sensitive data stored in a local SQLite database with no at-rest encryption applied (e.g. via SQLCipher), rather than in SharedPreferences/UserDefaults specifically.
Data correctly using the platform secure-storage API for one sensitive field (a password) but not another equally sensitive field (a session token, PII) stored alongside it in ordinary storage.
Data encrypted at rest but written in the clear to a temporary or cache file during use, readable for the duration of that operation.
mitigation: Store all genuinely sensitive data using the platform's secure-storage facility (EncryptedSharedPreferences/Android Keystore-backed storage, iOS Keychain) rather than ordinary SharedPreferences/UserDefaults or an unencrypted local database.
Where a local database holds sensitive data, apply database-level encryption (SQLCipher or platform-equivalent) with a key sourced from secure storage.
Minimize what sensitive data is cached locally at all — cache only what's operationally necessary, and prefer short-lived tokens over long-lived credentials or raw PII where possible.

Periodically audit all local-storage call sites for this pattern as part of routine mobile security assessments, since it's easy for a single sensitive field to be added to ordinary storage without following the same secure-storage convention used elsewhere.
MOBILE-010.mitigationClientFacing: Your app stores information on the device without adequate protection, so another app or anyone with access to the phone can read it. How serious this is depends on what is stored — settings are minor, credentials or personal data are not — so establishing the contents is the first step. Sensitive data should be encrypted at rest using the device's secure storage, and the app should avoid leaving readable copies in temporary or cache files while it works. This finding carries the most weight on shared or lost devices, where more people can reach the stored files.
MOBILE-010.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Insecure Local Data Storage” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: anyone with root or jailbreak access, an unencrypted device backup, or physical access plus forensic tools can read the data directly. Insecure local data storage is the most consistent mobile finding — sensitive data left readable on a lost or compromised device. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-011.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device with access to external/shared storage (an SD card, or Android's shared external storage partition). Standard file-system browsing (via `adb shell` or a file-manager app) — no root/jailbreak required, since external storage is, by definition, more broadly readable than the app's private sandbox.
MOBILE-011.whatItIs: The app saves sensitive cached files — downloaded documents, cached data containing personal info, temporary exports — to shared external storage on the device (historically readable by any app with basic storage permission), instead of its own private, sandboxed storage area.
MOBILE-011.rootCause: External storage is sometimes used just because it has more free space, or because one specific feature genuinely needs to place a file somewhere another app can reach it, like sharing a document. But that same external location often ends up reused for other, more sensitive files that were never meant to be reachable by other apps, without anyone going back to separate the two use cases.
MOBILE-011.impact: Any other app on the device with basic storage permission can read these files. On older Android versions in particular, that permission is broadly granted and very commonly requested, so this is not a high bar. No special privilege or user interaction is needed beyond that, exposing cached personal data, documents or API responses to any malicious or over-permissioned app sharing the phone.
stepsToIdentify: Use the application normally to trigger caching behavior (viewing a document, browsing content that gets cached) and monitor what files get written to external/shared storage locations.

Inspect the written files' content for sensitive data (PII, cached API responses, document content) rather than assuming external-storage writes are always for genuinely shareable/non-sensitive content.
From a separate, unprivileged test app (or a plain file-manager app) with only ordinary storage-read permission, attempt to read the same files to confirm cross-app accessibility.

Check the app's target SDK version and storage-access-framework usage, since scoped storage (introduced in more recent Android versions) narrows but doesn't always fully eliminate this exposure depending on how the app requests and uses storage access.
Confirm whether sensitive data is written to shared or external storage, which is readable by other apps and by anyone with device access.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes external-storage inspection during normal use of the test installation.
Trigger the app's caching behavior for representative sensitive content.
Locate the resulting cache files on external/shared storage.
From a separate app or file-manager context with only ordinary storage-read permission, read the same files to confirm cross-app accessibility.
Document the exact file location, content type, and the permission level required by another app to read it.
