Access-control attribute correctly configured for one sensitive item but inconsistently applied to another, equally sensitive item stored via the same API elsewhere in the app.
A secret placed in the secure store but with an access policy that does not require device unlock, leaving it readable while the device is locked.
mitigation: Configure every Keychain item with the most restrictive accessibility constant appropriate to its use (`kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly` at minimum, combined with a biometric access-control flag for the most sensitive items).
Generate every Android Keystore key intended to protect sensitive data with `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` and an appropriately short authentication-validity duration.
Audit all secure-storage API usage for consistent application of these access-control attributes across every sensitive item the app stores, not just the most obviously critical one.

Periodically re-test secure-storage configuration on a rooted/jailbroken device as part of routine mobile security assessments, since this class of gap is easy to introduce when a new sensitive field is added without following the established, more restrictive convention.
MOBILE-023.mitigationClientFacing: Your app does not consistently use the phone's dedicated secure store — the hardware-backed vault the platform provides for exactly this purpose — to hold its secrets, keeping some in ordinary app storage that lacks those protections. That makes the secrets easier to extract from a compromised or stolen device. The fix is to store all sensitive keys and tokens in the platform's secure store, configured to require the device be unlocked before they can be read. This is the correct home for secrets on a mobile device, and moving them there is a well-understood change.
MOBILE-023.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Insecure Keychain/Keystore Usage” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: depending on the exact gap, an attacker with a rooted or jailbroken device, or one who pulls a backup or device image, may retrieve the stored secret without unlocking the phone or passing biometrics at all. Improper credential and platform usage is a routine mobile finding, where secrets or permissions handled wrongly expose the user. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-024.prerequisites: The target application's manifest/Info.plist for custom URL-scheme registration review. A means to send a crafted URL to the test device (adb, or a link within a test web page/another app) targeting the registered scheme.
MOBILE-024.whatItIs: The app registers its own custom link format, such as 'myapp://', to handle certain actions. The code processing an incoming link does not properly check where that link came from before acting on it. It will accept sensitive actions — logging in, changing a setting — purely because a link said so, with no confirmation the link came from a trusted source rather than any random app or webpage.
MOBILE-024.rootCause: Custom link formats like this have no built-in way to prove which website or app is actually allowed to send them — unlike the newer, verified link system covered in a related finding. Any app on the phone, or any webpage in any browser, can build and trigger one of these links with whatever parameters it wants. If the app's handler trusts those parameters to perform something sensitive without double-checking where they came from, that link format becomes an open door anyone can knock on.
MOBILE-024.impact: Any malicious app, or any web page the victim visits, can trigger the sensitive action the custom link exposes. If that link is used as an OAuth-style callback without proper origin checks, it can silently sign the user into an account the attacker controls. It may also fire an unwanted in-app action, or change state outright — altering a setting or starting a transaction — purely because the victim clicked a link, with no informed consent to that specific action.
stepsToIdentify: Review the app's manifest/Info.plist for every registered custom URL scheme and decompile the corresponding handler code to understand what actions each URL path/parameter combination triggers.

Identify any handler that performs a sensitive, state-changing action (not just navigation to a screen) directly from URL parameters without an additional confirmation step or origin/source validation.

Craft a test URL replicating the sensitive action's parameter structure and trigger it via adb, a test web page, or a benign test app, observing whether the action executes without any additional user confirmation or source check.
Where the scheme is used for an OAuth-style redirect/callback, check specifically for state-parameter validation to rule out authorization-code interception/injection via this channel.
Enumerate the custom URL schemes the app registers and establish which trigger sensitive actions when opened.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes sending crafted custom-URL-scheme links to the test installation.
Identify a sensitive action reachable via the custom scheme's handler, based on the decompiled logic.
Construct a test URL replicating that action's expected parameters.
Trigger the URL via adb or a benign test web page/app and confirm the sensitive action executes without additional user confirmation or origin validation.
Document the exact URL scheme, path/parameters, and the sensitive action achieved without proper authorization.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate registered custom URL schemes
examplePayloads.command: apktool d target_app.apk -o decoded && grep -B5 -A5 'scheme=' decoded/AndroidManifest.xml

examplePayloads.label: Trigger a crafted deep link via adb
examplePayloads.command: adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "myapp://action/transfer?amount=100&to=attacker_account"

examplePayloads.label: Trigger the same link from a test web page to demonstrate a fully remote trigger
examplePayloads.command: echo 'Click' > poc.html

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate the app's registered URL schemes from its manifest or configuration
examplePayloads.command: aapt dump badging <app>.apk | grep -i scheme

variants: Custom scheme used as an OAuth redirect URI without state-parameter validation, enabling authorization-code interception/injection distinct from a direct sensitive-action trigger.

Sensitive action reachable via the custom scheme but requiring the app to already be in a specific, pre-authenticated session state, narrowing (but not eliminating) the practical attack window compared to a fully unauthenticated trigger.
A scheme that another app can also register, so the operating system may route the link to the attacker's app instead of the legitimate one.
mitigation: Require an additional, explicit user confirmation step within the app before executing any sensitive, state-changing action triggered via a custom URL scheme, regardless of the parameters supplied.
Prefer Android App Links/iOS Universal Links (which verify domain ownership) over custom URL schemes for any deep link that triggers sensitive functionality.
For OAuth-style flows, always validate the `state` parameter and use PKCE to prevent authorization-code interception/injection via the custom scheme.
Treat all custom-URL-scheme parameters as untrusted, externally-controllable input requiring the same validation rigor as any other unauthenticated input source.
MOBILE-024.mitigationClientFacing: Your app registers custom links that open it and perform actions, and those links are not adequately validated, so a crafted link — which a user could trigger by tapping something in a browser, message or another app — can drive the app into unintended behaviour. The fix is to treat everything arriving through such a link as untrusted input, validate it strictly, and require confirmation for any sensitive action. Note also that another app can register the same custom link, so the operating system may hand it to an attacker's app; the more robust verified-link mechanism avoids that and is preferable where available.
MOBILE-024.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Insecure URL Scheme / Deep Link Handling” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: any malicious app, or any web page the victim visits, can trigger the sensitive action the custom link exposes. Insufficient input/output validation is the mobile equivalent of the injection classes that dominate web breaches. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-025.prerequisites: The target application's APK. Standard Android tooling to decompile, modify, and re-sign an APK (apktool, apksigner or jarsigner with a self-generated test key) and a test device/emulator with developer options enabled to sideload the modified package.
MOBILE-025.whatItIs: The Android app can be taken apart, modified — say, to remove a security check or license verification — and re-signed with a completely different key, then reinstalled and run, all without the app or its backend ever noticing it's no longer the real, original app. That's because the app never checks its own signature against what it should actually be.
MOBILE-025.rootCause: Android allows any app package to be re-signed with any key and installed, as long as the user allows installs from outside the store. Unless the app specifically checks its own signature at runtime against a known-good value, there's nothing stopping a modified, re-signed copy of it from running — and the backend it talks to has no way to tell the difference either.
MOBILE-025.impact: An attacker can repackage the app with security checks stripped out, malicious code added, or licence and purchase validation removed, then distribute it through a third-party store or direct download. Users installing it have no way to tell it is not the official build. Any resulting credential theft, malware or fraud happens under the cover of the real app's name and branding.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the application and search for any runtime self-verification of its own signing certificate (comparing `PackageManager` signature info against an expected, hardcoded value).

If no such check is found, attempt to fully repackage the app: decompile with apktool, make a benign, easily-identifiable modification (e.g. a UI text change), and re-sign the resulting APK with a self-generated test key.
Install the repackaged, differently-signed APK on a test device and confirm whether it runs normally (or with the injected modification active) without any detection or refusal to run.

Where a signature-verification check does exist, assess its robustness — is it a simple, unobfuscated comparison that's itself trivially patchable out via the same repackaging process, or does it employ additional anti-tampering protection.
Confirm whether the app detects that it has been repackaged and re-signed, since without that check a tampered copy runs as though genuine.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes decompiling, modifying, re-signing, and running a repackaged version of the test installation.
Decompile the app, make a benign, clearly-identifiable modification (for demonstration purposes, not a genuinely malicious payload), and re-sign the resulting package with a test key.
Install the repackaged APK on a test device and confirm it launches and operates normally, with the injected modification active, despite the certificate mismatch from the original.

Where the app communicates with a backend, confirm the backend also has no server-side signature/attestation check (such as Play Integrity API) that would otherwise detect and reject the repackaged client.
Document the exact absence (or bypassability) of self-verification, and the resulting successful execution of the repackaged app.

examplePayloads.label: Decompile, modify, and repackage the APK
examplePayloads.command:
apktool d target_app.apk -o modified_app
# make a benign modification to modified_app/smali or resources
apktool b modified_app -o repackaged.apk

examplePayloads.label: Re-sign the repackaged APK with a test key
examplePayloads.command:
keytool -genkey -v -keystore test.keystore -alias testkey -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
apksigner sign --ks test.keystore --out repackaged_signed.apk repackaged.apk

examplePayloads.label: Install and run the repackaged, differently-signed APK
examplePayloads.command: adb install repackaged_signed.apk

examplePayloads.label: Confirm the app runs after being repackaged and re-signed with a different key
examplePayloads.command: # rebuild the app with a modified resource, re-sign it, install it, and observe whether it detects the change

variants: Repackaging used to remove a license/anti-piracy check versus repackaging used to inject genuinely malicious code (a credential-harvesting overlay) while preserving the app's original, legitimate-looking functionality and branding.
App-side signature check present but only enforced at one entry point, bypassable by patching out that specific check without needing to defeat any broader anti-tampering scheme.
Tamper detection present but implemented as a single check that can be located and neutralised in the decompiled code.
mitigation: Implement runtime self-verification of the app's own signing certificate against an expected, embedded value, refusing to run (or degrading functionality) if a mismatch is detected.

Use the platform's official integrity-attestation service (Google Play Integrity API, Apple's App Attest) to have the backend independently verify the client's authenticity server-side, rather than relying solely on client-side self-checks that can themselves be patched out.

Apply code obfuscation and anti-tampering protection specifically hardening the signature-verification logic itself, so it can't simply be patched out via the same repackaging process used to defeat other checks.
Monitor third-party app stores and known piracy/repackaging distribution channels for unauthorized, modified versions of the app circulating in the wild.
MOBILE-025.mitigationClientFacing: Your app does not detect when it has been taken apart, modified and repackaged, which means an attacker can distribute an altered version of your app — with added malicious behaviour or removed protections — that runs as though it were genuine. This is a particular risk for apps distributed or side-loaded outside the official stores. The fix is to have the app verify its own integrity and refuse to run if it has been repackaged and re-signed by someone other than you. Implemented as more than a single, easily-located check, this raises the effort required to produce a working tampered copy.
MOBILE-025.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Insufficient Anti-Tampering Against Repackaging” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: an attacker can repackage the app with security checks stripped out, malicious code added, or licence and purchase validation removed, then distribute it through a third-party store or direct download. Poor binary protections make it straightforward to decompile the app and recover hardcoded secrets or bypass client-side checks. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-026.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA. A decompiler (jadx, Ghidra, class-dump/Hopper) and a debugger/instrumentation framework (Frida, x64dbg-equivalent for mobile via jdb, or an iOS jailbreak debugger) to assess how readily the app yields to standard static and dynamic analysis.
MOBILE-026.whatItIs: The app ships with absolutely no protection against being analyzed or tampered with — no code obfuscation, no anti-debugging, no detection of rooted/jailbroken phones. Taking it apart reveals fully readable, near-original logic, and a debugger or tampering tool can attach to the running app with zero resistance.
MOBILE-026.rootCause: This kind of protection just wasn't prioritized during development — either the team didn't think reverse-engineering resistance mattered for this particular app, or building it in (through a commercial tool, or custom anti-debugging code) got pushed aside in favor of shipping features faster. The result is an app that's just as easy to analyze and modify as an unfinished development build.
MOBILE-026.impact: The absence of binary protection lowers the effort for nearly every other client-side attack on this list — tampering with business logic, extracting hardcoded secrets, bypassing pinning, defeating the biometric gate, repackaging the app. None of them need to defeat an anti-tampering layer first, because there isn't one. This finding is best understood as a multiplier on the app's other findings rather than something exploitable on its own.
stepsToIdentify: Attempt straightforward decompilation of the app and assess how close the output is to readable, near-original source code.
Attempt to attach a debugger/instrumentation framework (Frida) to a running instance and confirm no anti-debugging countermeasure triggers.

Check for any root/jailbreak detection logic at all, and if present, assess whether it's a simple, easily-bypassed check (a single file-existence test) versus a more layered, harder-to-defeat approach.
Assess whether any commercial or open-source obfuscator/RASP solution is applied at all, since even weak, defeatable protection is a materially different finding than none whatsoever.
Establish whether the binary carries any obfuscation or runtime self-protection, since its absence makes every other client-side finding easier to reach.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes static/dynamic analysis of the test installation's binary.
Decompile the app and demonstrate the ease of obtaining readable logic for a security-sensitive routine (a certificate-pinning check, a biometric callback) as evidence.
Attach Frida and confirm unhindered ability to hook functions and modify runtime behavior at will.

Where feasible within the engagement's scope, chain this finding into a concrete demonstration of one of the app's other client-side findings to show the practical consequence of the missing protection.
Document the specific absence of protection observed across decompilation, debugging, and root/jailbreak-detection dimensions.

examplePayloads.label: Assess decompilation readability
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk  # check whether logic is fully readable without significant manual reconstruction

examplePayloads.label: Confirm unhindered Frida attachment
examplePayloads.command: frida -U -n com.target.app -l enumerate_classes.js  # attach and enumerate app classes without any anti-instrumentation trigger

examplePayloads.label: Check for the absence of any root/jailbreak detection
examplePayloads.command: frida -U -n com.target.app -l check_root_detection_calls.js  # search for and confirm absence of common root-check APIs

examplePayloads.label: Confirm the app's logic is recoverable in readable form from the package
examplePayloads.command: # decompile the app package and confirm business logic and strings are readable

variants: Complete absence of any protection versus weak/outdated protection (a basic, single-check root-detection routine, or an old, publicly-defeated obfuscator) that provides negligible real-world resistance.

Obfuscation present but incomplete — string encryption and control-flow flattening applied to core logic while API keys or endpoint URLs remain in plaintext string constants, giving a reverse engineer an easy entry point despite the broader hardening effort.
Obfuscation applied to the app's own code but not to a bundled component that carries the sensitive logic or secrets.
mitigation: Apply a reputable commercial or well-maintained open-source obfuscation solution (ProGuard/R8 with aggressive settings at minimum, ideally a dedicated commercial obfuscator/RASP product for higher-sensitivity apps).
Implement layered root/jailbreak detection combining multiple independent indicators, understanding a sufficiently motivated attacker can still defeat any single-layer check.
Implement anti-debugging and anti-Frida countermeasures as defense in depth, accepting these raise attacker effort rather than providing an absolute guarantee.
Prioritize moving genuinely security-critical logic server-side rather than relying on binary protection alone to safeguard client-resident logic.
MOBILE-026.mitigationClientFacing: Your app has little protection against being taken apart and understood, which does not directly harm a user but makes every other weakness in the app easier for an attacker to find and exploit, and exposes its internal logic and any embedded secrets. Adding obfuscation and runtime self-protection raises the effort an attacker must spend. The more important principle, as with any client software, is that because the app can be fully understood and modified, it should never be trusted to enforce anything that genuinely matters — those controls belong on your servers, out of the attacker's reach.
MOBILE-026.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Insufficient Binary Protection” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: the absence of binary protection lowers the effort for nearly every other client-side attack on this list — tampering with business logic, extracting hardcoded secrets, bypassing pinning, defeating the biometric gate, repackaging the app. Poor binary protections make it straightforward to decompile the app and recover hardcoded secrets or bypass client-side checks. It is worth confirming and fixing early, before it is chained into something larger.

MOBILE-027.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device. A clipboard-monitoring utility or script (adb-based, or a separate benign test app polling the OS clipboard API) to demonstrate cross-application visibility of copied content.
MOBILE-027.whatItIs: A 'copy to clipboard' feature copies sensitive data — a password, a one-time code, a full card number — to the system clipboard, and never clears it afterward, and doesn't use the platform's option to mark that content as sensitive (which some newer phones support). That leaves the value readable by any other app that can read the clipboard, and sometimes even saved in a clipboard history feature.
MOBILE-027.rootCause: The clipboard is a shared resource across the whole phone that basically any app can read from — this feature was built without accounting for that, and without using the specific flag some platforms offer to protect genuinely sensitive content from being read by other apps or saved in clipboard history.
MOBILE-027.impact: Any other app on the device can silently read the value while it sits on the clipboard, including malware or an over-permissioned app that monitors clipboard activity. Where the operating system keeps a clipboard history, the value can persist there and stay readable for longer than the app's own clearing timeout would suggest — assuming it has one at all.
stepsToIdentify: Trigger the app's copy-to-clipboard feature for a sensitive value.
From a separate, independent test app or via `adb shell service call clipboard`, poll the clipboard immediately after the copy operation and confirm the sensitive value is readable.
Measure how long the value remains on the clipboard before (if ever) the app clears it.

Check whether the app marks the clipped content as sensitive using the platform's dedicated flag (where the target API level supports it), which suppresses clipboard-history/preview surfacing even though the raw value technically remains readable to a polling app.
Confirm whether the app places sensitive values on the shared clipboard and whether it clears them, since the clipboard is readable by every app.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes clipboard-monitoring testing against the test installation.
Trigger the copy-to-clipboard action for a sensitive value within the app.
From a separate monitoring app/script, capture the clipboard content immediately and confirm the sensitive value is present.
Check whether the platform's clipboard-preview/history feature (if present on the test OS version) also surfaces the value.
Document the exact sensitive data type exposed, the duration it remained accessible, and whether the sensitive-content flag was applied.

examplePayloads.command: adb shell service call clipboard 2 s16 com.android.shell

examplePayloads.label: Poll clipboard content from a benign test app after triggering the copy action in the target app
examplePayloads.command: # ClipboardManager.getPrimaryClip() polled from a separate test app immediately after switching from the target app

examplePayloads.label: Inspect the clipboard after the app copies a sensitive value
examplePayloads.command: # read the clipboard from a separate app after using the target app's copy action

examplePayloads.label: Locate clipboard usage in the decompiled source
examplePayloads.command: grep -rniE 'ClipboardManager|UIPasteboard|setPrimaryClip' <decompiled-src>/

variants: Sensitive value persisted in OS-level clipboard history/preview (a longer-lived, separate exposure on platforms with this feature) versus only the immediate, single-slot clipboard buffer.
Value copied automatically without explicit user action as a side effect of another feature, increasing the chance of inadvertent exposure.
A value the app clears after a delay but which universal-clipboard sync has already propagated to the user's other devices.
mitigation: Clear the clipboard automatically a short, fixed time after copying a sensitive value, and clear it immediately if the app is backgrounded before that timeout.
Use the platform's sensitive-clipboard-content API/flag where available to suppress clipboard preview/history surfacing of the copied value.
Minimize reliance on clipboard-based convenience features for highly sensitive values; where feasible, offer a masked, in-app "reveal" instead of a full clipboard copy.
Educate users, where the copy-to-clipboard feature is retained, that clipboard contents are shared system-wide and should be treated as temporarily exposed.
MOBILE-027.mitigationClientFacing: When your app copies a sensitive value such as a password or a one-time code to the clipboard for convenience, it leaves it there, where every other app on the device can read it — and on some platforms the clipboard is automatically synced to the user's other devices. The fix is to clear the clipboard shortly after copying a secret, and to recognise that clipboard sync can carry it further than intended, so the most sensitive values are better not placed on the clipboard at all. This is a small change with a real effect on devices exposed to untrusted apps.
MOBILE-027.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Pasteboard/Clipboard Leakage” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: any other app on the device can silently read the value while it sits on the clipboard, including malware or an over-permissioned app that monitors clipboard activity. Insecure local data storage is the most consistent mobile finding — sensitive data left readable on a lost or compromised device. It is worth confirming and fixing early, before it is chained into something larger.

MOBILE-028.prerequisites: A rooted/jailbroken test device or emulator with Frida and a root-hiding/bypass framework (Magisk Hide/Zygisk, or a Frida-based root-detection-bypass script set) available. The target application's decompiled code to locate its root/jailbreak-detection routine.
MOBILE-028.whatItIs: The app checks whether it's running on a rooted or jailbroken phone, and tries to restrict sensitive features if it is. But that check can be defeated using standard, publicly available tools — hooking the result of the check, using a well-known root-hiding tool, or just patching the check out of a modified copy of the app — letting the full, sensitive functionality run on a phone the developer specifically wanted to block.
MOBILE-028.rootCause: This kind of detection usually just looks for a small, well-known set of telltale signs — specific files, specific installed apps, specific system settings — and those are exactly what publicly available root-hiding tools are built to specifically hide or fake. Without extra layered protection around the check itself, it gets defeated by the same widely available tools that would beat almost any app relying on the same common checks.
MOBILE-028.impact: An attacker on a rooted or jailbroken device can defeat the app's attempt to restrict itself on exactly that kind of device. They then reach the sensitive functionality the developer deliberately withheld because of the elevated risk. The same root access also enables the attacks that restriction was meant to guard against, such as extracting protected secrets, hooking functions at runtime, and bypassing certificate pinning.
stepsToIdentify: Install and run the app on a rooted/jailbroken test device without any bypass tooling active, and confirm the app does detect the root/jailbreak state and restricts functionality as intended (establishing a baseline that detection exists at all).
Decompile the app to identify the specific indicators its detection logic checks for (file paths, package names, system properties).
Enable a standard root-hiding tool (Magisk Hide/Zygisk) or a Frida-based root-detection-bypass script and relaunch the app, observing whether the restriction is now bypassed.

Where the standard bypass doesn't immediately succeed, review whether the app's detection combines multiple independent indicators (making it more resistant) versus relying on a single, easily-spoofed check.
Confirm whether the app's root or jailbreak detection can be bypassed, since a bypass returns the app to full exposure on a compromised device.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes root/jailbreak-detection bypass testing against the test installation on a rooted/jailbroken test device.
Confirm the baseline: the app detects and restricts functionality on the rooted device without any bypass active.
Enable a standard root-hiding tool or Frida bypass script and relaunch the app.
Confirm whether the previously-restricted sensitive functionality is now accessible.
Document the specific bypass technique that succeeded and the functionality it unlocked.

examplePayloads.command: # Magisk app: add com.target.app to the Zygisk/DenyList, then relaunch the app

examplePayloads.label: Standard Frida-based root-detection bypass
examplePayloads.command:
objection -g com.target.app explore
android root disable

examplePayloads.label: Confirm whether the detection can be neutralised at runtime
examplePayloads.command: # attach an instrumentation toolkit and override the root/jailbreak check, then confirm the app proceeds

variants: Detection relying on a single, easily-spoofed indicator versus a layered approach combining multiple checks that resists standard, generic bypass tooling but may still be defeated with more targeted, app-specific reverse engineering.
Detection present in the app itself but not paired with any server-side attestation (Play Integrity API/App Attest) that could independently flag the device state to the backend.
Detection implemented as a single function whose result is checked once, allowing a one-line runtime override.
mitigation: Combine multiple independent root/jailbreak indicators rather than relying on any single, well-known check, increasing resistance to generic, off-the-shelf bypass tooling.

Use the platform's official integrity-attestation service (Google Play Integrity API, Apple's App Attest/DeviceCheck) to have the backend independently verify device integrity server-side, rather than relying solely on client-side detection that can itself be hooked/bypassed.
Apply anti-tampering protection specifically around the detection logic itself, so it can't simply be hooked or patched out via standard Frida scripting.

Accept that a sufficiently motivated attacker with a rooted/jailbroken device will likely eventually defeat any purely client-side detection, and ensure the most sensitive operations also have server-side verification independent of the client's self-reported device state.
MOBILE-028.mitigationClientFacing: Your app tries to detect when it is running on a compromised device — one that has been rooted or jailbroken, removing the operating system's normal protections — but that detection can be switched off by an attacker, returning the app to full exposure. Perfect detection is not achievable, so the mitigations raise the effort rather than guaranteeing it. The more durable position is not to rely solely on the device being intact: enforce anything that truly matters on your servers, and treat device-integrity detection as one signal among several rather than a dependable gate.
MOBILE-028.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Root/Jailbreak Detection Bypass” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: an attacker on a rooted or jailbroken device can defeat the app's attempt to restrict itself on exactly that kind of device. Poor binary protections make it straightforward to decompile the app and recover hardcoded secrets or bypass client-side checks. It is worth confirming and fixing early, before it is chained into something larger.

MOBILE-029.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device. Ability to trigger the OS's app-switcher/recent-apps view while the app displays representative sensitive data, and, for a rooted/jailbroken device, access to inspect any cached screenshot file the OS may have persisted.
MOBILE-029.whatItIs: When you switch away from the app (to another app or the home screen), the phone automatically takes a screenshot of whatever was on screen, to show in the recent-apps preview. If the app doesn't specifically hide its content right before this happens, sensitive information — an account balance, a message, a form full of personal data — ends up captured in that preview, and on some phones, even saved as a cached image file.
MOBILE-029.rootCause: This screenshot behavior is a standard phone feature the app doesn't control by default. Unless the app specifically opts in to hiding its content before going to the background (using a specific setting available on both major platforms), the screenshot just captures whatever was visible at that exact moment — including data the developer never intended to show up in a recent-apps preview or cached image.
MOBILE-029.impact: Anyone who can see the app-switcher view can read whatever was on screen when the app was backgrounded. That might be a bystander glancing over, or someone with brief access to an unlocked phone. Where the snapshot is also written to disk, an attacker with root access or a forensic tool can recover it long after the app has stopped running.
stepsToIdentify: Navigate to a screen displaying representative sensitive data within the app, then background the app (press home, or switch to another app) and open the OS app-switcher/recent-apps view.
Observe whether the sensitive data is visible in the app-switcher preview, versus the app showing a blank screen, its logo, or another obscured placeholder.
For a rooted/jailbroken test device, check the OS's cached-snapshot storage location for a persisted image file corresponding to the app and inspect its content directly.
Repeat across the app's various sensitive screens (not just the most obvious one), since obscuring behavior is sometimes applied inconsistently across different Activities/ViewControllers.
Confirm whether the operating system's app-switcher snapshot captures sensitive on-screen data, which then persists unprotected.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes app-switcher snapshot inspection on the test installation.
Navigate to a sensitive screen, populate it with representative test data, and background the app.
Open the app-switcher and document what sensitive content is visible in the preview.
On a rooted/jailbroken device, locate and inspect any persisted snapshot cache file for the same sensitive content.
Document each screen found to leak sensitive data via the app-switcher preview and/or a persisted cache file.

examplePayloads.command: adb shell find /data/system_ce/*/snapshots -iname '*com.target.app*'

examplePayloads.command: grep -rniE 'FLAG_SECURE|isSecureTextEntry|willResignActive' <decompiled-src>/

variants: Sensitive content visible in the live app-switcher preview but not persisted to a long-lived cache file (lower severity) versus content that's both visible in the preview and recoverable from a persisted snapshot file well after the app session ends.
Obscuring correctly applied on the primary/most obvious sensitive screen (a login form) but missed on a secondary screen (an in-app messaging view) added later in development.
Sensitive screens protected from the switcher snapshot but not from screenshots the user or another app can take.
mitigation: Apply the platform's screen-obscuring mechanism (Android's `FLAG_SECURE` on the window, or an iOS technique of swapping in a blank/branded placeholder view during `applicationDidEnterBackground`) on every screen displaying sensitive data.
Audit all sensitive screens in the app for consistent application of this protection, since it's easy to apply it to the most obvious screen and miss a secondary one added later.

Where `FLAG_SECURE` is used on Android, be aware it also blocks screenshots/screen-recording generally, which is a related, complementary protection worth applying deliberately rather than as an afterthought.
Periodically re-verify this behavior after OS updates, since app-switcher snapshot behavior can change subtly between platform versions.
MOBILE-029.mitigationClientFacing: When your app is sent to the background, the operating system takes a snapshot of its current screen to show in the app switcher, and that snapshot can capture sensitive information which then persists unprotected — visible to anyone who picks up the device. The fix is to mark sensitive screens so the system either blanks or masks them in the switcher snapshot. Consider screenshots as well, since a screen that is protected from the switcher may still be capturable by the user or another app, and the two protections are configured separately.
MOBILE-029.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Screen Caching / Sensitive UI Exposure” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: anyone who can see the app-switcher view can read whatever was on screen when the app was backgrounded. Insecure local data storage is the most consistent mobile finding — sensitive data left readable on a lost or compromised device. It is worth confirming and fixing early, before it is chained into something larger.

MOBILE-030.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device with device-level backup enabled (Android's auto-backup or `adb backup`, iOS's iCloud/iTunes/Finder backup). Standard backup-extraction tooling (`adb backup`/`abe`, or an iOS backup-parsing tool like iMazing or a manual plist/SQLite extraction from an unencrypted iTunes backup) to inspect the resulting backup archive's content.
MOBILE-030.whatItIs: The app's data gets automatically included in the phone's normal backup system without the app specifically excluding sensitive files from it. That means a full phone backup — whether stored in the cloud or locally — contains the same sensitive data the app stores on the device (credentials, tokens, cached personal info), and it can be pulled out of that backup without ever needing the original phone at all.
MOBILE-030.rootCause: Phone backup systems include everything by default unless a developer specifically excludes certain files or folders. That exclusion step is easy to forget, especially for data the app started saving after the initial backup setup was already done.
MOBILE-030.impact: Anyone with access to a device backup can extract the app's data without ever touching the original phone or getting past its lock screen. That backup might come from a stolen device, a compromised cloud account, or something as ordinary as a shared family cloud login. The backup is an independent copy of the same data, so every protection built around the device itself is simply sidestepped.
stepsToIdentify: Review the app's backup configuration (Android's `android:allowBackup` manifest attribute and any associated backup-rules XML, or iOS's file-exclusion attributes on sensitive files) to determine what is and isn't excluded from backup.
Generate a representative device backup (`adb backup` for Android, or an unencrypted iTunes/Finder backup for iOS) after populating the app with representative sensitive test data.
Extract and inspect the backup archive's content for the app's data, confirming whether sensitive fields identified during local-storage testing are present in the backup.
Where the app does declare specific backup-exclusion rules, verify they cover every genuinely sensitive file/data location the app uses, not just the most obvious one.
Confirm whether sensitive app data is included in device backups, which then leave the app's protected sandbox for the backup destination.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes device-backup generation and extraction testing against the test installation.
Populate the app with representative sensitive test data.
Generate a device backup and extract the app's data from the resulting archive.
Inspect the extracted data for plaintext or trivially-recoverable sensitive content.
Document the exact backup mechanism used, the specific sensitive data recovered, and the current backup-exclusion configuration (if any).

examplePayloads.label: Generate an Android device backup and extract the app's data
examplePayloads.command:
adb backup -f app_backup.ab com.target.app
java -jar abe.jar unpack app_backup.ab app_backup.tar

examplePayloads.label: Inspect the extracted backup archive for sensitive content
examplePayloads.command: tar -xvf app_backup.tar && grep -r 'password\|token' apps/com.target.app/

examplePayloads.label: Check Android manifest for backup configuration
examplePayloads.command: apktool d target_app.apk -o decoded && grep -i 'allowBackup\|fullBackupContent' decoded/AndroidManifest.xml

examplePayloads.label: Confirm whether the app excludes sensitive data from backup
examplePayloads.command: aapt dump xmltree <app>.apk AndroidManifest.xml | grep -iE 'allowBackup|fullBackupContent'

variants: Sensitive data excluded from backup correctly for one storage location (SharedPreferences) but not another (a local SQLite database) within the same app.

Backup exclusion correctly configured, but a genuine platform-level secure-storage item (Keychain, in iOS's default configuration) is nonetheless included in an iCloud Keychain sync the user didn't realize extended that far, a related but distinct exposure path.
Data correctly excluded from the platform backup but captured by a third-party backup component the app bundles.
mitigation: Explicitly exclude all files/data containing sensitive information from the platform's backup mechanism (Android's backup-rules XML with a `<exclude>` directive, or the `NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey` file attribute on iOS).

Where backing up some app data is genuinely desirable for user convenience (restoring app state on a new device), ensure only non-sensitive data is included, with genuinely sensitive fields re-derived or re-authenticated after restore instead.
Audit backup-exclusion configuration whenever new sensitive storage locations are added to the app, since this is a common regression point.

Where the platform's backup encryption itself may be disabled by the user (an unencrypted local iTunes backup, for example), treat backup content as equivalent in sensitivity to unencrypted local device storage when assessing risk.
MOBILE-030.mitigationClientFacing: Sensitive data from your app is included in the device's backups, which copies it out of the app's protected area and into the backup destination — a computer or a cloud account — where it is no longer under the app's protection. The fix is to exclude sensitive data from device backups so it stays within the app's secure storage. Check any third-party backup component the app bundles as well, since a common oversight is correctly excluding data from the platform's own backup while a bundled component copies it anyway.
MOBILE-030.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Sensitive Data in App Backups” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: anyone with access to a device backup can extract the app's data without ever touching the original phone or getting past its lock screen. Insecure local data storage is the most consistent mobile finding — sensitive data left readable on a lost or compromised device. It is worth confirming and fixing early, before it is chained into something larger.

MOBILE-031.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device with access to its logs (via `adb logcat` for Android, or the Console app/log streaming for iOS on a development-provisioned or jailbroken device). No special privilege beyond standard debugging log access is required on most development/test configurations.
MOBILE-031.whatItIs: The app writes sensitive data — passwords, session tokens, API keys, personal user information — directly into the phone's system log during normal use. This is usually leftover debug logging from development that never got removed or properly disabled before the app was published.
MOBILE-031.rootCause: Detailed logging gets added generously during development to help with debugging, and logging a variable's full value — including sensitive ones — sticks around into the released version because nothing systematically checks for this before release. On top of that, on many phones, any app with basic log-reading permission (or sometimes no special permission at all) can read another app's log output.
MOBILE-031.impact: Any app able to read the system log can read the logged data directly, on the Android versions and configurations where that remains possible. So can anyone who receives a bug report or log export that a user or support process shares. This exposes credentials, tokens or personal data through a channel most users, and plenty of developers, never think to check when reviewing how the app handles sensitive data.
stepsToIdentify: Use the app normally (log in, perform typical sensitive actions) while capturing the device log via `adb logcat` (Android) or a log-streaming tool (iOS).
Search the captured log for the app's package/process tag and inspect for sensitive-looking content (credentials, tokens, PII fields) rather than assuming logs are automatically safe.
Confirm whether the identified logging occurs in every build variant (including release) or only in a debug-specific build flavor that shouldn't reach production.
Check whether a third-party SDK bundled in the app is the source of any sensitive logging, distinguishing first-party logging statements from a dependency's own verbose-logging default.
Establish whether the app writes sensitive values to device logs, which are readable during development and via other channels on some platforms.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes device-log capture during normal use of the test installation.
Populate the app with representative sensitive test data through normal use while capturing the device log.
Search the captured log for the sensitive test data and confirm its presence in plaintext.

Where feasible, confirm cross-app log-read accessibility from a separate test app/adb session without special elevated privileges, to establish the practical exposure scope on the specific test device/OS version.
Document the exact log entries, the sensitive data type logged, and whether the issue is present in the release build specifically.

examplePayloads.label: Capture the device log while exercising the app's sensitive functionality
examplePayloads.command: adb logcat | grep -i 'com.target.app'

examplePayloads.label: Search a captured log for common sensitive-data patterns
examplePayloads.command: adb logcat -d | grep -iE 'password|token|api[_-]?key|ssn'

examplePayloads.label: Check whether logging occurs in the release build specifically
examplePayloads.command: grep -rn 'Log\.' decompiled_output/ | grep -v 'BuildConfig.DEBUG'

examplePayloads.label: Capture the app's log output and inspect for sensitive values
examplePayloads.command: # capture device logs while exercising the app and search for tokens, credentials or personal data

variants: Sensitive logging present only in a debug build flavor that was inadvertently distributed instead of the intended release build, versus logging present unconditionally regardless of build type.
Sensitive logging originating from a bundled third-party SDK's own verbose-logging default rather than first-party application code.
Sensitive values absent from the app's own logs but written by a bundled component that logs verbosely without redaction.
mitigation: Remove all logging of sensitive data from the codebase, or gate any genuinely necessary verbose logging behind a build-type check (`if (BuildConfig.DEBUG)`) that's guaranteed to be false in release builds.
Add automated static analysis to the CI/CD pipeline to flag logging statements referencing known-sensitive variable names/patterns before a release build is produced.
Review and configure third-party SDKs' logging verbosity explicitly, disabling verbose/debug logging in the production build configuration.
Where log data is genuinely needed for production diagnostics, redact/mask sensitive fields before logging rather than logging the raw value.
MOBILE-031.mitigationClientFacing: Your app writes sensitive information — potentially including credentials, tokens or personal data — to the device's logs, which are readable during development and, on some platforms, reachable through other channels. Logs are meant for diagnostics, not secrets, and sensitive values reach them easily by accident. The fix is to remove sensitive values from everything the app logs, and to check bundled third-party components, which frequently log verbosely without redacting. This is easy to overlook precisely because logging feels harmless, but it quietly relocates protected data into an unprotected place.
MOBILE-031.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Sensitive Data in Logs” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: any app able to read the system log can read the logged data directly, on the Android versions and configurations where that remains possible. Insecure local data storage is the most consistent mobile finding — sensitive data left readable on a lost or compromised device. It is worth confirming and fixing early, before it is chained into something larger.

MOBILE-032.prerequisites: The target application and a second, malicious-simulation test app installed on the same Android test device. Ability to build a benign, clearly-labeled overlay test app using the `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW` permission to draw over the target app's UI.
MOBILE-032.whatItIs: A malicious app using Android's 'draw over other apps' permission can place an invisible or deceptive overlay on top of the real app's sensitive buttons — a login button, a permission prompt, a payment confirmation — tricking the user into thinking they're tapping the overlay's fake content, when their tap is actually registering on the real app's hidden button underneath. This works because the real app doesn't have any protection against being covered by an overlay.
MOBILE-032.rootCause: Android's 'draw over other apps' permission lets an app place persistent content on top of anything else, including sensitive screens. Unless the underlying app explicitly turns on a specific setting that ignores taps landing on an obscured view, a tap on a covered element is still delivered as a normal, valid tap — with no warning to the user that what they tapped may not have been what they saw.
MOBILE-032.impact: An attacker first gets the user to install a harmless-looking app that asks for the overlay permission — something users are well conditioned to grant for screen dimmers and floating widgets. That app can then cover the real app's buttons with deceptive content. The user taps what they think they see and unknowingly authorises something else: granting a dangerous permission, confirming a payment, or accepting a security prompt.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the app's most sensitive UI interactions — permission-grant dialogs, payment confirmations, security-setting toggles — as the priority targets for this check.
Decompile the app and check whether `setFilterTouchesWhenObscured(true)` (or the equivalent `android:filterTouchesWhenObscured` view attribute) is applied to these sensitive views.
Build or use an existing benign overlay test app (requesting `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW`) and, with the target app's sensitive screen in the foreground, draw a full-screen or targeted overlay over it.
Attempt to tap through the overlay at the location of the underlying sensitive button and confirm whether the tap registers on the target app despite the visual obstruction.
Confirm whether the app permits another app to draw over it, which lets an overlay capture taps intended for the real interface.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes overlay-based tapjacking testing against the test installation using a benign test overlay app.
Grant the test overlay app the `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW` permission (simulating a user who has granted this to a seemingly innocuous app).
Navigate the target app to a sensitive screen and activate the test overlay, positioned to visually obscure the sensitive button with deceptive content.

Tap at the screen location of the underlying sensitive button (as visually indicated by the overlay's deceptive prompt) and confirm whether the target app registers the tap as if the user had directly interacted with its real UI.
Document which specific sensitive UI elements lack overlay-touch-filtering protection and the resulting successful tapjacking demonstration.

examplePayloads.label: Check decompiled code for overlay-touch-filtering protection on sensitive views
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d decompiled_output target_app.apk && grep -rn 'setFilterTouchesWhenObscured\|filterTouchesWhenObscured' decompiled_output/

examplePayloads.label: Build a minimal overlay test app requesting SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW
examplePayloads.command: # minimal Android app: request SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, add a WindowManager overlay view with deceptive content positioned over the target app's known button coordinates

examplePayloads.label: Grant the overlay permission and activate the overlay for testing
examplePayloads.command: adb shell appops set com.test.overlayapp SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW allow

examplePayloads.label: Locate overlay-protection settings and confirm they cover sensitive screens
examplePayloads.command: grep -rniE 'filterTouchesWhenObscured|FLAG_WINDOW_IS_OBSCURED' <decompiled-src>/

variants: Full-screen deceptive overlay versus a narrow, precisely-positioned overlay covering only the specific sensitive button, the latter being harder for a user to notice as suspicious.
Overlay attack targeting a system permission-grant dialog specifically (tricking the user into granting a dangerous permission to a different, malicious app) rather than an in-app sensitive action.
An overlay that does not capture taps but obscures a security prompt, tricking the user into approving an action they cannot see.
mitigation: Apply `setFilterTouchesWhenObscured(true)` (or the equivalent view attribute) to every sensitive interactive view in the app, causing Android to silently discard touch events delivered while the view is obscured by another app's overlay.
For the most sensitive confirmations, consider an additional, deliberate friction step (a swipe-to-confirm gesture, a re-authentication prompt) that's harder to trigger via a simple, redirected tap.

Educate users generally about the risk of granting the "draw over other apps" permission to unfamiliar apps, though this is a weaker, awareness-based mitigation relative to the app-side technical control.

Test overlay-touch-filtering protection on every new sensitive UI element added in future releases, since this is easy to miss for a newly-added button if it isn't part of an established, reviewed pattern.
MOBILE-032.mitigationClientFacing: On Android, your app can be covered by an overlay drawn by another app, which lets a malicious app capture taps meant for your interface or trick the user into approving something they cannot properly see — the digital equivalent of a fake keypad placed over a real one. The fix is to have sensitive screens refuse to act on taps when they are being obscured by another app's overlay. This requires a malicious app to be present, so its severity depends on that, but it is a well-known technique for stealing input and approvals, and the protection is a specific, supported setting.
MOBILE-032.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Tapjacking / Overlay Attacks” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: an attacker first gets the user to install a harmless-looking app that asks for the overlay permission — something users are well conditioned to grant for screen dimmers and floating widgets. Security misconfiguration such as a debuggable release build hands an attacker with the device far more than intended. It is worth confirming and fixing early, before it is chained into something larger.

MOBILE-033.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA for dependency extraction. A software-composition-analysis (SCA) tool (MobSF, OWASP Dependency-Check, or a mobile-specific SCA scanner) capable of identifying bundled third-party libraries/SDKs and their versions.
MOBILE-033.whatItIs: The app bundles third-party libraries or SDKs — analytics, ads, networking, UI components — at outdated versions that have known, publicly documented security bugs, because the app's dependency setup locks in a specific version once and there's no ongoing process to review and update it as new vulnerabilities get discovered.
MOBILE-033.rootCause: Third-party SDKs typically get integrated once and left alone unless a specific feature update is needed, since updating a dependency carries its own risk of something breaking and needing retesting. Without a dedicated, recurring process to review dependencies, the locked-in version quietly accumulates known, unpatched vulnerabilities over the app's lifetime — the same pattern that shows up with any outdated software dependency.
MOBILE-033.impact: Any known flaw in the outdated library becomes exploitable against the app, provided the app's own use of that library actually reaches the vulnerable code. The range is wide. It might sit in a code path the app never calls, which makes it low risk. Or it might be directly reachable, such as a TLS flaw in a networking library or a parsing bug in a data-handling one.
stepsToIdentify: Extract the list of bundled third-party libraries and their versions from the APK/IPA (via its dependency manifest, or by fingerprinting bundled library binaries/resources).
Run a software-composition-analysis tool against the extracted dependency list and review the resulting CVE findings, prioritizing Critical/High severity issues with a known public exploit.

For any Critical/High CVE found, assess reachability — whether the app's actual usage of the library invokes the vulnerable code path, or the vulnerable functionality is present but unused — to prioritize remediation accurately.
Cross-reference the library's pinned version against its current, actively-maintained release to quantify how far behind the integration has drifted.
Inventory the third-party components the app bundles and check each against published vulnerability advisories for its version.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes dependency extraction and SCA scanning of the test installation's app package.
Run the SCA tool against the extracted dependency list and record the full CVE findings list with severity ratings.
For the highest-severity, most-reachable finding, research whether a public proof-of-concept exists for that specific CVE in the context of a mobile app integration.

Where safe and clearly scoped, demonstrate the specific vulnerability against a non-production test build of the app (rather than the production release) to confirm real-world exploitability rather than relying on the scanner's severity rating alone.
Document the specific library, its version drift from current, and the prioritized CVE list with reachability assessment for the report.

examplePayloads.label: Run a mobile-focused software-composition-analysis scan against the APK
examplePayloads.command: mobsf-cli scan target_app.apk --format json > sca_results.json

examplePayloads.label: Fingerprint bundled library versions from extracted app resources
examplePayloads.command: unzip -o target_app.apk -d extracted && find extracted -iname '*.properties' -exec grep -H 'version' {} \;

examplePayloads.label: Cross-reference a specific bundled library's version against known CVEs
examplePayloads.command: grep -A5 '"library-name"' sca_results.json

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate bundled third-party components and their versions
examplePayloads.command: # extract the app's dependency manifest and list bundled components with their versions

variants: Vulnerable library present but its vulnerable code path not actually reachable by the app's specific usage pattern (lower practical risk despite a high CVSS score) versus one actively invoked in the app's core functionality.
Vulnerability introduced via a transitive dependency of a directly-integrated SDK, requiring dependency-tree-level scanning rather than only checking the top-level, directly-integrated libraries.
A vulnerable component present but not reachable through the app's own use, which lowers but does not remove the risk if another path reaches it.
mitigation: Establish a recurring dependency-audit process (ideally automated via CI/CD-integrated SCA scanning) to catch newly-disclosed CVEs against bundled libraries promptly rather than only during periodic external assessments.
Update outdated third-party libraries/SDKs to their current, patched versions on a regular cadence, budgeting for the associated regression-testing effort as a routine maintenance cost.
Where a specific SDK has a poor security-maintenance track record, evaluate replacing it with a better-maintained alternative rather than continuing to accept its accumulating risk.
Maintain a software bill of materials (SBOM) for the app's bundled dependencies to make future vulnerability cross-referencing faster and more reliable.
MOBILE-033.mitigationClientFacing: Your app includes third-party components that contain known, published security flaws, each with a fix already available in a newer version. Attackers look for exactly these, because the weaknesses are documented and reliable, and a flaw in a bundled component is a flaw in your app. The fix is to update the affected components to current versions and to make dependency scanning a routine part of your build process, so outdated components are caught before release. Prioritise components whose vulnerable functionality your app actually uses, while still planning to update the rest.
MOBILE-033.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Third-Party SDK / Library Vulnerabilities” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: any known flaw in the outdated library becomes exploitable against the app, provided the app's own use of that library actually reaches the vulnerable code. Inadequate supply-chain security in bundled SDKs has repeatedly shipped malicious or leaky third-party code inside otherwise trusted apps. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-034.prerequisites: A mobile application using a backend-as-a-service platform for its database, storage or authentication. The application package, from which project identifiers and API keys can be extracted. A client or HTTP access to the platform's REST interface. Authorisation to query the backend directly using credentials recovered from the application.
MOBILE-034.whatItIs: These platforms let a mobile client talk to the database directly, which removes the server tier and with it the place authorisation usually lives. Access control instead lives in a rules document that the developer writes. Rules default to permissive during development, and the application works identically whether they were ever tightened, so the omission produces no symptom. The client's API key is embedded in the app and is not a secret.
MOBILE-034.rootCause: The development-friendly default is open access, and the documentation's quick-start reflects that. Tightening rules requires modelling every access pattern precisely, which is real work with no visible payoff, so it is deferred. Developers also frequently treat the embedded API key as a credential, when it identifies the project rather than authorising the caller. Rules changes are made in a console rather than in the repository, so they escape code review.
MOBILE-034.impact: Anyone who extracts the project identifier from the application — which requires only unzipping it — can query the backend directly, bypassing the app entirely. Where read rules are open the whole dataset is retrievable, and where write rules are open records can be modified or destroyed. Storage buckets with open rules disclose user-uploaded content. The access uses the platform's own API, so it appears as ordinary client traffic.
stepsToIdentify: Extract the application package and locate the platform configuration file containing project identifiers and keys.
Identify which platform services are in use: database, storage, authentication, functions.
Query the database REST endpoint unauthenticated and record whether data is returned.
Repeat as an authenticated but unprivileged user, since rules frequently distinguish only between signed-in and anonymous.
Enumerate storage paths and test whether objects are listable and readable without authorisation.
Test write access with a benign record, since read and write rules are configured independently.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers direct backend queries using identifiers recovered from the application.
Unzip the package and extract the platform configuration.
Issue an unauthenticated read against a collection path observed in the application's traffic or code.
Where reads succeed, establish the scope of exposure by counting records rather than retrieving them all.
Create an account through the application's normal registration and retry, since many rules only require any signed-in user.
Test a single benign write to a dedicated test path and remove it immediately, confirming write exposure without altering real data.

examplePayloads.label: Extract configuration
examplePayloads.command: unzip -o app.apk -d app_out && grep -rhoE '"project_id"|"firebase_url"|"storage_bucket"|apiKey' app_out/res app_out/assets 2>/dev/null | sort -u

examplePayloads.label: Unauthenticated database read
examplePayloads.command: curl -s 'https://<project>.firebaseio.com/.json?print=pretty' | head -40

examplePayloads.label: Collection read via REST
examplePayloads.command: curl -s 'https://firestore.googleapis.com/v1/projects/<project>/databases/(default)/documents/users'

examplePayloads.label: Storage listing
examplePayloads.command: curl -s 'https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/<bucket>/o'

examplePayloads.label: Authenticated-user retry
examplePayloads.command: # register through the app, then repeat the same reads with the resulting ID token

examplePayloads.label: Controlled write test
examplePayloads.command: curl -sX PUT 'https://<project>.firebaseio.com/pentest_marker.json' -d '{"probe":"MOB-RULES-1"}' && curl -sX DELETE 'https://<project>.firebaseio.com/pentest_marker.json'

variants: Rules requiring only an authenticated user, where anyone who registers reaches every user's data.
A storage bucket with open listing, disclosing uploaded documents and images belonging to all users.
Cloud functions callable directly without the authorisation the application performs client-side.
A second project used for staging with open rules and real data copied into it.
mitigation: Write rules that authorise per document against the requesting user's identity, and deny by default.
Treat the embedded API key as a public project identifier rather than as a credential.
Keep rules in version control and review them as code, rather than editing them in a console.
Test rules with the platform's emulator and rule-testing tooling as part of the build.
Apply the same rule discipline to storage paths, including listing permission.
Never copy production data into a project whose rules are relaxed for development.
MOBILE-034.mitigationClientFacing: The security rules on your app's cloud backend — the service that stores and serves your users' data — are configured too permissively, so data can be read or changed by users who should not be able to. Because the mobile app talks to this backend directly, weak rules here expose data regardless of how well the app itself is built. The fix is to tighten the backend rules so each user can reach only their own data and only in the ways intended, enforced by the backend rather than by the app. This is a common and high-impact misconfiguration and warrants prompt review.
MOBILE-034.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Insecure Backend-as-a-Service Security Rules” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: anyone who extracts the project identifier from the application — which requires only unzipping it — can query the backend directly, bypassing the app entirely. Improper credential and platform usage is a routine mobile finding, where secrets or permissions handled wrongly expose the user. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-035.prerequisites: A mobile application whose backend makes trust assumptions about the client, such as rate limits enforced in the app, client-side eligibility checks, or business flows assumed to require the real application. A rooted or jailbroken test device or emulator. Authorisation to run a modified client and to call backend endpoints directly.
MOBILE-035.whatItIs: Attestation is how a backend gains evidence that the request came from an unmodified application on a genuine device. Without it, the backend cannot distinguish its own app from a script replaying the same API calls. Root and jailbreak detection implemented inside the app does not fill the gap, because that check runs in the environment it is trying to assess and can be patched out. The distinction is whether the evidence is produced by something the attacker controls.
MOBILE-035.rootCause: Attestation requires backend integration and introduces failure modes on legitimate devices, so it is often skipped in favour of client-side checks that are cheap to add. Those checks feel equivalent because both produce a boolean, but one is self-reported. Where attestation is implemented, a common error is verifying the token in the app rather than at the server, which moves the decision back into the attacker's environment.
MOBILE-035.impact: Anything the backend delegates to the client stops being enforced: rate limits, eligibility rules, in-app purchase validation, promotional constraints. Automated abuse at scale becomes practical because the attacker needs no device at all once the API is understood. For applications with a financial or loyalty component, this is direct fraud exposure. It also invalidates the assumption that traffic reaching the API came from a user interacting with a screen.
stepsToIdentify: Determine whether the application requests any attestation token and whether the backend requires one.
Locate root or jailbreak detection in the binary and establish whether its result influences any server-side decision.
Identify which controls are enforced only in the client: rate limits, eligibility, validation of purchases.
Test whether backend endpoints accept requests from a plain HTTP client with no attestation token.
Where an attestation token is sent, determine whether the server validates it or merely logs it.
Check whether the token is bound to the specific request, or can be captured once and replayed.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers running a modified client and calling the API directly.
Intercept the application's traffic and record a normal request sequence for a controlled business flow.
Replay the sequence from a standalone client with no application present and record whether it succeeds.
Where a token is required, capture one and test whether it is accepted on a second, different request.
Patch out the client-side root detection and confirm the application functions, demonstrating the check is not server-enforced.
Demonstrate a client-side control being bypassed, choosing the least consequential available flow.

variants: Attestation verified inside the application rather than at the server, which leaves the decision in the attacker's environment.
A token accepted without nonce binding, so one valid token authorises unlimited requests.
Attestation required on some endpoints and not others, where the unprotected ones do the same work.
Purchase receipts validated client-side, letting a modified client grant itself entitlements.
mitigation: Verify attestation tokens server-side, and require them on every endpoint where client integrity matters.
Bind each attestation token to a server-issued nonce and to the specific request, so tokens cannot be replayed.
Enforce rate limits, eligibility and validation server-side regardless of what the client does.
Validate purchase receipts against the store's server API rather than trusting the client.
Treat root and jailbreak detection as telemetry that raises suspicion, never as a control.
Decide deliberately how to handle attestation failure, since a permissive fallback removes the control entirely.
MOBILE-035.mitigationClientFacing: Your backend cannot tell whether a request genuinely comes from your unmodified app on a real device, or from a modified copy, an automated script, or an emulator. That lets an attacker interact with your service outside the app's intended constraints — bypassing client-side limits and protections wholesale. The fix is to add device and app attestation, so your servers can verify the request originates from a genuine, untampered app before honouring sensitive operations. This underpins the trust your server places in the app, and without it every client-side control can be sidestepped by not using your client.
MOBILE-035.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Absent Device and App Attestation Allowing Modified Clients” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: anything the backend delegates to the client stops being enforced: rate limits, eligibility rules, in-app purchase validation, promotional constraints. Poor binary protections make it straightforward to decompile the app and recover hardcoded secrets or bypass client-side checks. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-036.prerequisites: A mobile application authenticating through an OAuth or OpenID Connect flow that returns to the app via a custom URL scheme, app link or universal link. A test device where a second application can be installed to claim the same scheme. Authorisation to install a tester-built application and to intercept the authorisation response.
MOBILE-036.whatItIs: The authorisation code comes back to the application through a redirect, and on mobile the redirect target is a scheme or link the operating system routes. Custom schemes are not exclusive: any application can register the same one, and on Android the resolution when two apps claim a scheme is not guaranteed to favour the legitimate one. Without PKCE, an intercepted code can be exchanged for tokens by whoever holds it.
MOBILE-036.rootCause: Custom schemes were the original mobile redirect mechanism and remain common because they work everywhere without the domain verification that app links require. PKCE solves interception but is optional in many libraries and omitted in older integrations. Embedded web views are also still used despite giving the host application visibility of the credentials entered. The authorisation server frequently permits loose redirect matching, which widens the target.
MOBILE-036.impact: An attacker's application installed on the same device intercepts the authorisation code and exchanges it for the victim's tokens, yielding full account access without ever seeing a password. The victim's experience is a normal login, because the legitimate authorisation happened. Where an embedded web view is used, a malicious or compromised host application observes the credentials directly, which is worse than interception of a code.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the redirect mechanism: custom scheme, app link with domain verification, or an embedded web view.
Determine whether PKCE is used, and whether the code challenge method is SHA-256 rather than plain.
Check whether the state parameter is generated unpredictably and validated on return.
Where app links are used, verify that domain association is correctly published and validated.
Test whether a second application registering the same scheme can receive the redirect.
Review the authorisation server's registered redirect URIs for wildcards or loose matching.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers installing a tester application on the test device.
Capture a complete authorisation flow and record the redirect URI, state and any code challenge.
Build a minimal application registering the same custom scheme and install it alongside the target.
Initiate authentication in the target application and record which application receives the redirect.
Where the code is intercepted, attempt the token exchange, which succeeds without PKCE and fails with it.
Report the redirect mechanism, PKCE status and interception result together, since the severity depends on the combination.

examplePayloads.command: grep -A3 -E 'android.intent.action.VIEW' app_out/AndroidManifest.xml | grep -oE 'android:scheme="[^"]+"' | sort -u

examplePayloads.command: # inspect the authorization request for code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256
