examplePayloads.label: Capture the redirect
examplePayloads.command: adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d 'myapp://callback?code=TEST&state=TEST'

examplePayloads.label: Token exchange attempt
examplePayloads.command: curl -sX POST https://idp.example.test/oauth/token -d 'grant_type=authorization_code&code=<intercepted>&client_id=<id>&redirect_uri=myapp://callback'

examplePayloads.label: App link verification
examplePayloads.command: adb shell pm get-app-links <package>

variants: An embedded web view rather than the system browser, letting the host application observe credentials directly.
A loosely matched redirect URI at the authorisation server, permitting a redirect to an attacker-controlled path.
A public client with an embedded client secret, which is recoverable from the package.
State omitted or predictable, permitting cross-site request forgery against the authorisation flow.
mitigation: Use PKCE with the SHA-256 challenge method on every mobile authorisation request.
Prefer verified app links or universal links over custom schemes, since domain verification makes the target exclusive.
Use the system browser or a secure custom tab rather than an embedded web view.
Generate state unpredictably and validate it on return, rejecting mismatches.
Register exact redirect URIs at the authorisation server and disable wildcard matching.
Treat the mobile client as public: never embed a client secret and never rely on one for security.
MOBILE-036.mitigationClientFacing: The way your app handles sign-in through an external identity provider mishandles the return step, in a way that could let an attacker intercept the sign-in and gain access to a user's account. This sits at the front door of your app's authentication, so a weakness here can undermine account security broadly. The fix is to handle the sign-in return securely — strictly validating where it is sent and confirming it matches the request that began it — following the current recommended pattern for mobile sign-in. Given that it concerns account takeover, this warrants prompt attention.
MOBILE-036.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Insecure OAuth Redirect Handling in Mobile Applications” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: an attacker's application installed on the same device intercepts the authorisation code and exchanges it for the victim's tokens, yielding full account access without ever seeing a password. Insecure authentication/authorization on mobile lets a tampered client bypass checks the server should have enforced. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-037.prerequisites: An Android application exposing a content provider, whether explicitly exported or reachable through a granted URI permission. A test device and a tester-built application to act as the querying client. Authorisation to query the provider from another application and to attempt parameter injection against it.
MOBILE-037.whatItIs: A content provider is an interface other applications can query, and the query parameters — selection strings, sort order, projection — are frequently passed into a database query with string concatenation. That is SQL injection with an inter-application interface as the entry point. File-backed providers have the analogous problem: a path supplied by the caller is resolved without normalisation, so traversal reaches files outside the intended directory.
MOBILE-037.rootCause: The provider API hands the developer a selection string and a sort order, which invites concatenation into the query. Selection arguments exist to parameterise this but are optional and frequently unused. Providers are sometimes exported unintentionally, since older Android versions defaulted to exported when an intent filter was present. File providers resolve caller-supplied paths against a base directory without canonicalising first, which traversal defeats.
MOBILE-037.impact: A malicious application installed on the device reads the target application's private database, which commonly holds session tokens, personal data and cached records. Injection into the selection clause reaches tables the provider never intended to expose. Path traversal in a file provider reads arbitrary files in the application's sandbox, including shared preferences and credential caches. All of this requires no special permission on the attacking application.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate providers declared in the manifest and record which are exported and what permissions they require.
Identify providers exported implicitly, including those reachable through granted URI permissions.
Determine the authority and the URI paths the provider serves.
Query the provider from a separate application and record whether access is permitted.
Test whether the selection, projection and sort parameters are concatenated by supplying values with SQL metacharacters.
For file-backed providers, test whether traversal sequences in the path escape the intended directory.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers querying the provider from a tester-built application on the test device.
Enumerate provider authorities and attempt a baseline query to establish reachability.
Inject a condition into the selection parameter and observe whether the result set changes, which proves concatenation.
Use the projection parameter to reach columns or tables outside the provider's intended exposure.
For a file provider, request a path with traversal sequences and confirm whether a file outside the base directory is returned.
Record what was retrievable by category rather than extracting personal data in bulk.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate providers
examplePayloads.command: grep -E '<provider' -A6 app_out/AndroidManifest.xml

examplePayloads.label: Baseline query
examplePayloads.command: adb shell content query --uri content://com.example.app.provider/records

examplePayloads.label: Selection injection
examplePayloads.command: adb shell content query --uri content://com.example.app.provider/records --where "1=1) OR (1=1"

examplePayloads.label: Projection abuse
examplePayloads.command: adb shell content query --uri content://com.example.app.provider/records --projection "* FROM sqlite_master--"

examplePayloads.label: File provider traversal
examplePayloads.command: adb shell content read --uri content://com.example.app.fileprovider/files/../shared_prefs/session.xml

examplePayloads.label: Automated provider testing
examplePayloads.command: drozer console connect -c "run app.provider.query content://com.example.app.provider/records"

variants: A provider protected by a permission declared at normal rather than signature level, which any application can request.
A grant-URI-permission path that is broader than intended, exposing more than the shared item.
An openFile implementation that resolves a caller-supplied path without canonicalisation.
A provider that is not exported but is reachable through an exported activity acting as a proxy.
mitigation: Set exported to false explicitly on every provider that does not need to serve other applications.
Protect necessary providers with a signature-level permission so only the developer's own applications can query them.
Use parameterised selection arguments and never concatenate caller-supplied values into a query.
Validate the projection against an allowlist of permitted columns rather than passing it through.
Canonicalise any caller-supplied path and confirm it resolves inside the intended directory before opening it.
Expose the narrowest surface the use case requires, rather than a general-purpose query interface over the database.
MOBILE-037.mitigationClientFacing: A data-sharing component in your Android app can be manipulated through crafted input to reach data or files it should not, including files elsewhere on the device that the app can access. This lets a malicious app on the device extract information through your app. The fix is to validate all input to these components strictly, use parameterised queries for any database access, and confine file access to the specific intended locations rather than trusting the path supplied. This requires a malicious app to be present, but it is a direct route by which one app uses another to reach protected data.
MOBILE-037.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Content Provider Injection and Path Traversal” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: a malicious application installed on the device reads the target application's private database, which commonly holds session tokens, personal data and cached records. Insufficient input/output validation is the mobile equivalent of the injection classes that dominate web breaches. That direct line to impact is why it warrants prompt confirmation and remediation on any live system.

MOBILE-038.prerequisites: A mobile application handling credentials, tokens, payment details or personal data. A rooted or jailbroken test device permitting process memory access, or the ability to capture a memory dump. Authorisation to dump and search process memory, and a handling procedure for any sensitive values recovered.
MOBILE-038.whatItIs: Values are protected carefully on disk and in transit and then left in memory indefinitely. Strings in managed runtimes are immutable, so a password held in a string cannot be overwritten and persists until garbage collection happens to reclaim it, which may be long after the login screen closed. Anything in memory is recoverable from a process dump, and on a compromised device that is a straightforward operation.
MOBILE-038.rootCause: Language runtimes do not provide a way to erase an immutable string, and the byte-array alternatives are awkward enough that developers use strings anyway. Values are also copied during normal processing — into logs, into UI state, into serialisation buffers — so even careful clearing of the original leaves copies behind. Memory hygiene has no visible effect in testing, so it is rarely prioritised.
MOBILE-038.impact: On a rooted or compromised device, or via a crash dump collected by a diagnostics service, credentials and tokens are recoverable long after the user believed the session ended. This defeats the protection given to the same values at rest, since the memory copy is unencrypted by definition. Where payment data is involved the retention itself may breach the applicable standard, independent of whether anyone extracted it.
stepsToIdentify: Identify which sensitive values the application handles and at what point each should no longer be needed.
Establish whether values are held as immutable strings or as clearable byte arrays.
Dump process memory after authentication and search for marker credentials used during the test.
Repeat after logout and after backgrounding the application, to determine whether values are cleared on those transitions.
Check whether crash reporting captures memory regions, since that transmits the same data off the device.
Determine whether the application requests exclusion from memory capture where the platform supports it.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers memory dumping and agree how recovered values will be handled and destroyed.
Authenticate with distinctive marker credentials so recovered values are unambiguous and not real.
Dump the process memory while the session is active and search for the markers.
Log out within the application, dump again, and record whether the markers persist.
Background the application, wait, dump again, and record persistence across the lifecycle.
Report which value types persist and for how long, rather than reproducing recovered values.

examplePayloads.command: frida -U -n com.example.app -e 'Memory.scanSync(...)'   # or use objection: memory dump all

examplePayloads.label: Objection memory search
examplePayloads.command: objection -g com.example.app explore -c 'memory search "MARKER-MOB-5" --string'

examplePayloads.label: Full dump for offline search
examplePayloads.command: objection -g com.example.app explore -c 'memory dump all /tmp/app.dump'

examplePayloads.label: Search the dump
examplePayloads.command: strings -n 8 /tmp/app.dump | grep -c 'MARKER-MOB-5'

variants: Tokens retained after logout because only the on-disk copy is cleared.
Payment card data persisting in memory after the transaction completes.
Sensitive values captured in a heap dump uploaded by a crash reporting service.
Decrypted database contents held in memory long after the records were displayed.
mitigation: Hold secrets in mutable byte arrays and overwrite them explicitly once they are no longer needed.
Minimise the lifetime of sensitive values, clearing them at the earliest point rather than at session end.
Clear credentials and tokens on logout and when the application is backgrounded, not only on process termination.
Use platform key stores for cryptographic operations so key material never enters application memory.
Exclude sensitive regions from crash reports, or disable memory capture in crash reporting entirely.
Accept that memory protection is mitigation rather than prevention on a compromised device, and pair it with server-side session controls.
MOBILE-038.mitigationClientFacing: Your app holds sensitive values in the device's memory longer than necessary, which leaves a window in which they could be recovered from a compromised device or captured if memory is written to disk. Some persistence is unavoidable, but it should be minimised: the app should overwrite sensitive values as soon as it is finished with them rather than leaving them to linger. This is a lower-severity finding for most apps, but it rises in importance for apps handling high-value data on devices that may be rooted, jailbroken or otherwise compromised.
MOBILE-038.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Sensitive Data Retained in Application Memory” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: on a rooted or compromised device, or via a crash dump collected by a diagnostics service, credentials and tokens are recoverable long after the user believed the session ended. Insecure local data storage is the most consistent mobile finding — sensitive data left readable on a lost or compromised device. It is worth confirming and fixing early, before it is chained into something larger.

MOBILE-039.prerequisites: A mobile application with input fields receiving sensitive data: credentials, payment details, identifiers or personal information. A test device where the keyboard's learned dictionary and autofill store can be inspected, which may require root or a backup extraction. Authorisation to inspect keyboard caches and autofill stores.
MOBILE-039.whatItIs: Text typed into an application does not stay within it. The keyboard is a separate application that receives every keystroke, and unless the field is marked appropriately it adds words to a learned dictionary to improve prediction. Autofill frameworks may store field contents. Third-party keyboards can transmit what they learn to their own servers. So a value the application protects carefully can end up cached by software the developer never chose.
MOBILE-039.rootCause: Learning is the keyboard's default behaviour because prediction is its purpose, and the application must opt out per field using the correct input type or flag. Developers set input types for keyboard layout rather than for privacy, so a field configured for a numeric pad may still be learned. Autofill participation is likewise opt-out per field. Users install third-party keyboards freely, and the application has no control over what they do.
MOBILE-039.impact: Sensitive values persist in a store the application cannot reach and does not clear, surviving application uninstall and appearing as suggestions in unrelated applications — which is also how the exposure is typically discovered. On a shared or compromised device the cache is readable directly. Where a third-party keyboard transmits learned text, the data leaves the device to a party the organisation never assessed, which is a disclosure independent of any attacker.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate input fields receiving sensitive data and record the input type and flags set on each.
Confirm whether password and sensitive fields use an input type that disables suggestions and learning.
Check whether autofill is disabled on fields where it should not participate.
Type distinctive marker values into each field and then check whether they appear as suggestions elsewhere.
Inspect the keyboard's learned dictionary directly where device access permits.
Determine whether the application warns about or restricts third-party keyboards on sensitive screens.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers inspecting keyboard and autofill stores on the test device.
Enter unique marker values into each sensitive field through normal application use.
Open an unrelated application and begin typing the marker prefix to see whether it is suggested.
Where device access permits, inspect the keyboard dictionary and autofill store directly for the markers.
Record which fields leaked and which did not, since the difference identifies the misconfigured ones.
Report per field, because remediation is a per-field attribute change rather than a global setting.

examplePayloads.label: Review input types
examplePayloads.command: grep -E 'inputType|importantForAutofill|textNoSuggestions' -r app_out/res/layout | grep -i -E 'password|card|pin|ssn'

examplePayloads.label: Correct password configuration
examplePayloads.command: android:inputType="textPassword"   android:importantForAutofill="no"

examplePayloads.label: Numeric sensitive field
examplePayloads.command: android:inputType="numberPassword"   <!-- not "number", which is still learned -->

examplePayloads.label: Marker entry
examplePayloads.command: # enter MARKERALPHA, MARKERBETA and so on into successive sensitive fields

examplePayloads.label: Suggestion check
examplePayloads.command: # in an unrelated app, type MARKER and record which markers are offered as suggestions

examplePayloads.label: Dictionary inspection
examplePayloads.command: adb shell run-as <keyboard.package> ls -la databases/ 2>/dev/null   # requires a debuggable keyboard or root

variants: A third-party keyboard transmitting learned text to its own servers, taking the data off the device entirely.
Autofill storing payment or identity values in a store shared across applications.
Clipboard retention where the user copies a sensitive value and it remains available to other applications.
An iOS field lacking the secure text entry flag, leaving it subject to the same learning behaviour.
mitigation: Set an input type that disables suggestions and learning on every sensitive field, including numeric ones.
Disable autofill participation on fields that should not be stored, using the platform's per-field attribute.
Use secure text entry on iOS for sensitive fields, which also suppresses learning.
Clear the clipboard after a sensitive value is copied, and avoid offering copy on such fields.
Consider restricting third-party keyboards on high-sensitivity screens where the platform allows it.
Test with markers as part of release testing, since the misconfiguration is per field and easy to reintroduce.
MOBILE-039.mitigationClientFacing: Sensitive information users type into your app — passwords, card numbers, personal details — can be captured and retained by the device's keyboard suggestions, autofill and predictive-text features, which then store it outside your app's control and may surface it elsewhere. The fix is to mark sensitive input fields so the operating system excludes them from these learning and caching features. This is a small, specific change per field, and it matters because the data leaves your app's protection through a channel neither you nor the user is thinking about while they type.
MOBILE-039.realWorldContext: On mobile application assessments, “Sensitive Input Cached by Keyboards, Autofill and Predictive Text” is a finding that surfaces more often than clients expect. The stake is real: sensitive values persist in a store the application cannot reach and does not clear, surviving application uninstall and appearing as suggestions in unrelated applications — which is also how the exposure is typically discovered. Insecure local data storage is the most consistent mobile finding — sensitive data left readable on a lost or compromised device. It is worth confirming and fixing early, before it is chained into something larger.

MOBILE-040.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA and a rooted/jailbroken test device or emulator. A network intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/mitmproxy) with the CA installed and any certificate pinning bypassed (objection/Frida) so third-party SDK traffic is visible. A decompiler (jadx) and MobSF for static SDK inventory. Authorization to intercept and inspect the app's outbound traffic on a test account.
MOBILE-040.whatItIs: The app bundles third-party analytics and advertising SDKs (e.g. Facebook, Firebase/Google Analytics, AppsFlyer, Adjust, a crash reporter) and hands them personal data — email, phone number, precise location, device identifiers, or in-app behavior — before the user has consented, or beyond what they agreed to. The data leaves the app to servers the developer does not control, often on app launch, so the user has no visibility into who receives it or why.
MOBILE-040.rootCause: SDKs are dropped in for growth analytics, attribution, and monetization, and their default configuration is deliberately data-hungry: many auto-collect identifiers and events the moment they initialize. Developers wire user attributes into these SDKs for segmentation without gating the calls behind a consent check, and initialization frequently happens in Application.onCreate before any consent screen is shown. No one audits what actually goes over the wire versus what the privacy policy claims.
MOBILE-040.impact: Personal data is disclosed to third parties without a lawful basis, which is both a privacy harm and a regulatory exposure (GDPR, CCPA, India's DPDP Act). An attacker or malicious partner receiving the feed can correlate a real identity to behavior; a network attacker who sees the requests can harvest the same PII. Because collection fires before consent, the app is non-compliant from first launch, and the data cannot be recalled once transmitted.
MOBILE-040.realWorldContext: This is one of the most common privacy findings in real mobile engagements, and it has driven enforcement rather than just crashes. Regulators fined multiple health and menstruation-tracking apps after they were found forwarding intimate user data to Facebook's SDK via automatic app events, and a wave of GDPR complaints targeted apps that initialized Google and Facebook SDKs before showing a consent banner. On engagements you typically see it as an app that fires an analytics 'user_properties' or 'app_open' event carrying the logged-in email and precise GPS on launch, long before the cookie/consent dialog appears. The business consequence is regulatory fines and app-store policy takedowns, not a technical exploit.
stepsToIdentify: Run MobSF or `jadx` over the APK and inventory bundled analytics/ad SDKs (grep for `com.facebook`, `com.google.android.gms.analytics`, `com.appsflyer`, `com.adjust`, `io.branch`, crash reporters) to know which third parties are in scope.

Proxy the app through Burp/mitmproxy with pinning bypassed and capture all traffic from a cold launch through login, noting every distinct third-party host contacted before any consent prompt is accepted.

Inspect the payloads to those hosts for PII: email, phone, name, precise latitude/longitude, advertising ID (AAID/IDFA), Android ID, or hashed-but-linkable identifiers, and record which fields go where.
Decline or ignore the app's consent/privacy prompt (or use a fresh install) and confirm whether analytics/ad calls still fire — pre-consent transmission is the core of the finding.

Cross-reference the observed data flows against the app's own privacy policy and store listing (Apple Privacy Nutrition Label / Google Data Safety section) to identify undeclared collection or sharing.
Check SDK initialization in decompiled code (`Application.onCreate`, Firebase `setUserProperty`, `AppEventsLogger`) to confirm the calls are unconditional rather than gated on a stored consent flag.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes traffic interception and PII-flow analysis against the test installation and test account.
Perform a clean install, launch the app, and observe outbound requests before touching any consent control — capture the first analytics/attribution beacons.
Log in with the test account and trigger location-using and profile screens, then identify each request that carries user PII or a persistent identifier to a third-party domain.
Decode and document the specific fields leaked per recipient (e.g. Facebook `custom_events` with `em` hashed email, Firebase `up.email`, AppsFlyer `device.gaid` + `customer_user_id`).
Demonstrate the pre-consent nature by repeating the launch with consent explicitly declined and showing the same beacons still transmit.
Document each third-party recipient, the exact PII sent, whether it preceded consent, and the mismatch against the stated privacy policy / store data-safety declaration.

examplePayloads.label: Capture third-party hosts contacted before consent (mitmproxy)
examplePayloads.command: mitmdump -s <(echo 'def response(f):\n  print(f.request.host, f.request.path)') --set block_global=false  # launch app cold, note hosts hit pre-consent

examplePayloads.label: Burp filter to isolate PII in outbound SDK traffic

examplePayloads.label: Decode a Firebase Analytics measurement payload
examplePayloads.command: curl -s 'https://app-measurement.com/a' --data-binary @captured_body.bin -o /dev/null -v  # inspect the 'up.' user-property and 'ep.' event-param keys carrying email/location in the captured body

examplePayloads.label: Frida hook to log values passed into the Facebook events SDK
examplePayloads.command: frida -U -n com.target.app -e 'Java.perform(function(){var L=Java.use("com.facebook.appevents.AppEventsLogger");L.logEvent.overload("java.lang.String","android.os.Bundle").implementation=function(n,b){console.log("[FB]",n,b?b.toString():"");return this.logEvent(n,b);};});'

variants: Consent is collected but ignored — the SDK initializes and transmits regardless of the stored consent flag, so the toggle is cosmetic.
PII is 'hashed' (e.g. SHA-256 email for Facebook Advanced Matching) but sent anyway, which is still identifiable linkage and undeclared sharing rather than true anonymization.
A crash-reporting SDK (Crashlytics/Sentry) attaches the logged-in user's email and last-viewed screen content to every crash report as breadcrumbs, leaking PII through the error channel.
Attribution SDKs collect the Android AAID / iOS IDFA plus install referrer and forward them to an ad network before the ATT/consent prompt is answered.
mitigation: Defer all analytics/ad/attribution SDK initialization until after the user has granted explicit, granular consent, and never call SDK init in `Application.onCreate` unconditionally.
Gate every `logEvent`/`setUserProperty`/attribution call behind a persisted consent state, and provide a genuine opt-out that stops transmission rather than only hiding a toggle.

Stop passing PII into analytics/ad SDKs entirely — use non-identifying, app-generated pseudonymous IDs for analytics, and disable SDK auto-collection features (Firebase `firebase_analytics_collection_enabled=false` by default, Facebook `AutoLogAppEventsEnabled=false`).
Data-minimize: collect only fields with a defined purpose, disable precise-location and advertising-ID collection unless essential, and honor platform signals (iOS ATT, Android AD_ID permission).
Reconcile the app's actual data flows with its privacy policy and the store data-safety/nutrition-label declarations, and add a release-gate traffic review so undeclared PII egress fails the build.
Prefer server-side or first-party analytics for sensitive contexts so raw PII never leaves the developer's trust boundary to a third party.
MOBILE-040.mitigationClientFacing: Your app shares users' personal information — things like their email, location, or a device advertising ID — with outside analytics and advertising companies, and in some cases it does so the moment the app opens, before the user has agreed to anything. Users cannot see this happening and did not choose it, which is both a trust problem and, in most regions, a legal one. The fix is to hold off on starting these third-party tools until the user has genuinely consented, to stop feeding them personal details at all where you can, and to make sure what your app actually sends matches what your privacy policy and app-store listing promise. This matters because once data has left to a third party you can no longer control or recall it.

MOBILE-041.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA and a decompiler (jadx/apktool for Android, class-dump/Info.plist inspection for iOS). A test device or emulator to observe runtime permission prompts and actual data access. Optionally Frida to trace which APIs are actually called. Authorization to review the app's manifest, entitlements, and runtime behavior.
MOBILE-041.whatItIs: The app requests far more access than its features justify — reading all contacts, precise background location, the full photo library, SMS, call logs, or the microphone — and then collects the data those permissions unlock even where the feature does not need it. A weather app asking for the contact list, or a flashlight-style utility requesting location, is the recognizable shape: the permission grant becomes a standing licence to harvest personal data.
MOBILE-041.rootCause: Permissions accrete over an app's life as features are added and rarely removed when features are cut, and SDKs sometimes declare permissions the host app never intended. Product teams request broad access 'to be safe' or to enable future functionality, and coarse-grained platform permissions (a single CONTACTS grant exposes the entire address book) mean a small feature can demand disproportionate access. There is often no periodic audit tying each declared permission to a live, necessary feature.
MOBILE-041.impact: Once granted, the permission lets the app read and potentially exfiltrate large volumes of personal data — every contact, continuous location history, all photos with their embedded GPS metadata — well beyond what the user reasonably expected when they tapped Allow. This expands the app's data footprint and breach blast radius, creates regulatory exposure for collecting data without a purpose, and hands any compromise of the app (or a bundled malicious SDK) access to the user's entire address book or movements.
MOBILE-041.realWorldContext: Excessive-permission over-collection is the pattern behind a long line of app-store purges and enforcement actions: Google and Apple have repeatedly pulled apps that requested contacts, SMS, or call-log access unrelated to their function, and the notorious 'flashlight app wants your location and contacts' meme is a real permission-abuse category. In engagements the classic finding is a utility or content app that declares READ_CONTACTS and ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION, uploads the full address book on first launch 'to find friends', and keeps precise location running in the background for ad targeting. The consequence is usually a compliance and reputational hit — regulators treat purposeless collection as unlawful even when nothing is 'hacked'.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the APK and list every permission in `AndroidManifest.xml` (or the iOS `Info.plist` usage-description keys and entitlements), separating dangerous/runtime permissions from normal ones.

Map each declared dangerous permission to a concrete, user-visible feature that requires it, flagging any permission with no corresponding feature (e.g. READ_SMS, READ_CALL_LOG, ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION, READ_CONTACTS in an app that never displays them).
Identify permissions pulled in transitively by third-party SDKs via merged-manifest analysis, since these are often broader than the app itself needs.

On device, exercise the app's features while monitoring which protected APIs are actually invoked (Frida trace, or Android 12+ permission-usage/Privacy Dashboard) to distinguish declared-but-unused from actively-used permissions.
For location specifically, determine whether the app requests precise (FINE) where coarse would suffice, and whether it requests background access for a foreground-only feature.
Confirm whether granting a permission triggers bulk collection — e.g. the entire contact list uploaded on grant rather than a single contact chosen via a picker.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes permission and data-collection review against the test installation.
Enumerate the declared permission set and produce the permission-to-feature justification map, listing each unjustified or over-broad permission.

Grant the questionable permissions on the test device and observe, via proxy and Frida, what data the app reads and whether it transmits it (e.g. POST of the full contacts array to a backend on grant).
For location, verify the app collects precise/background location and quantify how often and to where it is sent versus what the feature needs.
Demonstrate the gap between least-privilege alternatives (contact picker, coarse location, scoped photo access) and the app's chosen broad grant.
Document each excessive permission, the data it exposes, whether that data is actively collected/transmitted, and the least-privilege alternative that would satisfy the feature.

examplePayloads.command: aapt dump permissions target_app.apk  # or: apktool d target_app.apk -o out && grep -i 'uses-permission' out/AndroidManifest.xml

examplePayloads.label: Read iOS purpose strings and entitlements
examplePayloads.command: plutil -p Payload/TargetApp.app/Info.plist | grep -iE 'UsageDescription|Location|Contacts|Photo' ; codesign -d --entitlements :- Payload/TargetApp.app

examplePayloads.label: Trace actual contacts access at runtime with Frida
examplePayloads.command: frida-trace -U -n com.target.app -j '*ContentResolver!query'  # observe queries against ContactsContract to see if the full address book is read

examplePayloads.label: Capture bulk contact upload on permission grant
examplePayloads.command: # Burp: after tapping Allow on the contacts prompt, look for a POST (e.g. /v1/contacts/sync) whose body contains the device's full contact list

examplePayloads.label: Inspect merged manifest for SDK-injected permissions (Android)
examplePayloads.command: grep -rn 'uses-permission' app/build/outputs/logs/manifest-merger-*-report.txt  # or review AndroidManifest.xml in the built APK and attribute each permission to its source

variants: Background location requested for a feature that only needs location while the app is open (foreground), enabling continuous movement tracking.
Full photo-library access requested where the platform's scoped/limited photo picker would let the user share only the specific images needed.
A dangerous permission declared only because a bundled SDK requires it, collecting data on the SDK's behalf that the host app has no feature for.
Coarse feature, precise data: requesting FINE location or full-contact read when the feature would work with COARSE location or a single user-picked contact.
mitigation: Audit every declared permission against a concrete live feature and remove any permission with no current justification, including ones inherited from SDKs (use `tools:node="remove"` in the manifest for SDK-injected permissions).

Adopt least privilege at the API level: use the system contact picker and Android Photo Picker / iOS limited-library selection so the app touches only the item the user chose rather than the whole collection.
Request the narrowest capability that works — COARSE instead of FINE location, foreground-only instead of background — and justify each with a clear in-context rationale prompt.
Request permissions just-in-time at the point of use rather than up front, so users can tie the grant to a feature and deny access to unrelated ones.
Data-minimize collection behind a granted permission: read only what the feature needs at the moment, avoid bulk sync of entire address books or photo sets, and set retention limits.
Add a periodic permission review to the release process and keep the store data-safety/privacy-label declaration in sync with the actual, minimized permission set.
MOBILE-041.mitigationClientFacing: Your app asks for access to more of the user's personal information than its features actually use — for example the whole contact list, all photos, or the user's location at all times — and in some cases collects that data even though nothing in the app needs it. Users tend to grant these requests without realizing how much they are handing over, which enlarges the amount of personal data you hold and are responsible for protecting. The fix is to ask only for what each feature genuinely requires, to ask at the moment the feature is used so the request makes sense, and to take only the specific item the user picked rather than sweeping up everything. This reduces both your privacy risk and the damage if the app is ever compromised.

MOBILE-042.prerequisites: The target application's APK/IPA on a rooted/jailbroken device or emulator, with a network proxy (Burp/mitmproxy) and certificate pinning bypassed to read outbound traffic. jadx/MobSF for static analysis of identifier-collection code. On iOS, the ability to observe ATT (App Tracking Transparency) prompt behavior. Authorization to intercept traffic on a test account.
MOBILE-042.whatItIs: The app collects persistent tracking identifiers — the Google Advertising ID (AAID), Apple's IDFA, the Android ID (SSAID), or hardware identifiers — and sends them to advertising, attribution, or analytics endpoints, often bundled with other data, without proper consent or in a way the user cannot reset. Because these identifiers are stable across sessions and shared across apps and networks, leaking them lets third parties link a person's activity across many different apps into a single profile.
MOBILE-042.rootCause: Advertising IDs exist to enable attribution and ad targeting, and SDKs read them by default. The problems arise when the app transmits the AAID/IDFA before consent (or without the required iOS ATT authorization), pairs it with other PII so it stops being pseudonymous, or falls back to non-resettable identifiers (Android ID, IMEI-derived values, MAC-based fingerprints) precisely so tracking survives a user resetting their advertising ID. Platform rules that forbid this are not enforced in the app's own code.
MOBILE-042.impact: A resettable advertising ID that is transmitted alongside an email or account ID becomes a permanent, identity-linked tracker, defeating the user's ability to opt out or reset it. Multiple apps and ad networks receiving the same identifier can merge behavior into a cross-app profile, and a network attacker who observes the traffic can single out and follow a specific device. Where non-resettable identifiers are used as a fallback, the tracking cannot be escaped at all, which violates platform policy and privacy law and risks app-store removal.
MOBILE-042.realWorldContext: Identifier leakage is the mechanism that makes cross-app ad tracking work, and it is exactly what Apple's App Tracking Transparency and Google's move to restrict the AAID were designed to curb. Security researchers regularly find apps that keep transmitting the IDFA after the user chose 'Ask App Not to Track', or that quietly build a device fingerprint (Android ID + build props + install list) so a reset advertising ID no longer breaks the link — a technique that got several SDKs banned from the App Store. On engagements the tell-tale finding is an attribution beacon carrying the AAID plus the logged-in customer ID to an ad network on launch, sometimes with a non-resettable Android ID as a 'backup key'. The stakes are platform-policy takedowns and privacy fines.
stepsToIdentify: Statically search decompiled code for identifier-collection APIs: `AdvertisingIdClient.getAdvertisingIdInfo` (AAID), `Settings.Secure.ANDROID_ID`, `getDeviceId`/IMEI, `Build.SERIAL`, and iOS `ASIdentifierManager.advertisingIdentifier` / `identifierForVendor`.
Proxy the app and capture outbound requests, searching payloads for the device's actual AAID/IDFA value and any Android ID / hardware identifier to see which endpoints receive them.
Check whether the identifier is sent together with PII (email, account ID, phone) in the same request or session, which converts a pseudonymous ID into an identity-linked tracker.
On iOS, respond 'Ask App Not to Track' to the ATT prompt (or verify no prompt is shown) and confirm whether the IDFA is still transmitted despite the denied authorization.

Look for a fingerprinting fallback: collection of stable, non-resettable signals (Android ID, installed-package list, build fingerprint, screen metrics) used to re-identify the device after an advertising-ID reset.
Reset the advertising ID on the device and repeat capture to confirm whether tracking genuinely resets or the app re-links via a stored/fallback identifier.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes traffic interception and identifier-flow analysis against the test installation and test account.
Record the device's real AAID/IDFA (Settings > Google/Privacy) as a search string, then capture app traffic from cold launch through login.
Locate every request carrying that identifier, note the recipient hosts, and flag any that are third-party ad/attribution domains.
Show identity linkage by finding a request where the advertising ID and an account-level PII field travel together.
On iOS, deny ATT and demonstrate continued IDFA transmission if present; on Android, reset the AAID and show the app re-identifies the device via a fallback identifier.
Document each identifier collected, its resettability, the recipients, whether transmission respected consent/ATT, and any PII pairing that defeats pseudonymity.

examplePayloads.label: Find identifier-collection calls in decompiled code
examplePayloads.command: jadx -d out target_app.apk && grep -rniE 'getAdvertisingIdInfo|ANDROID_ID|getDeviceId|Build.SERIAL|advertisingIdentifier|identifierForVendor' out/sources/

examplePayloads.label: Search intercepted traffic for the device advertising ID
examplePayloads.command: # Burp/mitmproxy: search all requests for the device's real AAID/IDFA string to enumerate every endpoint it is sent to

examplePayloads.label: Frida hook to log AAID reads and their callers (Android)
examplePayloads.command: frida-trace -U -n com.target.app -j 'com.google.android.gms.ads.identifier.AdvertisingIdClient$Info!getId'

examplePayloads.label: Detect non-resettable Android ID usage
examplePayloads.command: frida -U -n com.target.app -e 'Java.perform(function(){var S=Java.use("android.provider.Settings$Secure");S.getString.implementation=function(r,k){var v=this.getString(r,k);if(k=="android_id")console.log("[ANDROID_ID read]",v);return v;};});'

examplePayloads.label: Confirm IDFA still sent after ATT denial (iOS)
examplePayloads.command: # Deny the ATT prompt, then in the proxy confirm whether the (should-be-zeroed) IDFA is still populated and transmitted to attribution hosts

variants: IDFA transmitted despite the user selecting 'Ask App Not to Track' in the iOS ATT prompt, violating the platform tracking policy.
Advertising ID paired with a hashed email or account ID in the same beacon, making the 'resettable, pseudonymous' identifier permanently identity-linked.
Device-fingerprinting fallback (Android ID + install list + build fingerprint) used to re-link the device after an advertising-ID reset, defeating the reset control.
Use of the non-resettable Android ID (SSAID) or a hardware identifier as the primary tracking key instead of the resettable advertising ID.
mitigation: Do not collect or transmit advertising identifiers until the user has consented, and on iOS gate all IDFA use on a granted ATT authorization; treat a denied/undetermined status as no tracking.
Never pair the advertising ID with account-level PII; keep advertising-context data pseudonymous and separate from identity data.
Do not use non-resettable identifiers (Android ID, IMEI, serial, MAC) for tracking or as a fallback re-identification key — respect the user's ability to reset their advertising ID.
Remove device-fingerprinting logic and configure SDKs to disable identifier auto-collection where not strictly required (and honor Android's `com.google.android.gms.permission.AD_ID` gating).
Encrypt all traffic and pin certificates so identifiers cannot be harvested by a network observer, and minimize which endpoints receive any identifier at all.
Keep the store data-safety/privacy-label 'tracking' declarations accurate and add a traffic review to the release gate to catch identifier leakage before shipping.
MOBILE-042.mitigationClientFacing: Your app collects the kind of identifier that advertising and analytics companies use to follow a device from app to app, and it shares that identifier in ways the user has not agreed to — in some cases even after they asked not to be tracked, and in some cases using an identifier the user cannot reset. Combined with the user's email or account, this turns an ID that is supposed to be anonymous and resettable into a permanent tag tied to a real person. The fix is to only use these identifiers after genuine consent, to never combine them with personal details, and to never fall back to identifiers the user cannot clear. This keeps you within Apple's and Google's rules and out of privacy-enforcement trouble.

MOBILE-043.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device with a test account holding representative PII. For Android: `adb` and (for `allowBackup=true` apps) `adb backup`/Android Backup Extractor, or filesystem access on a rooted device. For iOS: a local unencrypted iTunes/Finder backup and a backup browser, or filesystem access on a jailbroken device. jadx/apktool to review the manifest backup flags. Authorization to extract and inspect app data.
MOBILE-043.whatItIs: The app writes personal data — names, email/phone, addresses, date of birth, government IDs, message history, precise location, or profile details — into local files (SharedPreferences, plists, SQLite databases, JSON caches) in plaintext, and does not exclude that data from device backups. Because Android's `allowBackup` and iOS's default backup behavior copy app data off the device, the PII ends up in unencrypted backups on a computer or in the cloud, where it can be extracted without ever unlocking the app.
MOBILE-043.rootCause: Local storage is treated as private and therefore 'safe enough', so developers store PII in the clear rather than encrypting it, and leave `android:allowBackup` at its permissive default (or omit the iOS 'do not back up' / Data Protection attributes). The threat model overlooks that backups, a lost/stolen unlocked device, another app with storage access, or a rooted/jailbroken phone can all reach that data outside the app's own access controls.
MOBILE-043.impact: Anyone who can obtain a device backup — a shared or compromised computer, an attacker with brief physical access via `adb backup`, or access to an unencrypted cloud backup — can extract the user's full PII without the app's authentication ever coming into play. On a lost, stolen, or malware-infected device the plaintext files are directly readable. This exposes exactly the sensitive personal data users trust the app to safeguard, with regulatory consequences where the data includes identity documents or health-adjacent details.
MOBILE-043.realWorldContext: Plaintext PII in backups is a recurring high-impact finding because it bypasses every in-app protection at once. The classic Android case is an app shipping `android:allowBackup="true"` (still the default on older target SDKs) so that a simple `adb backup` over USB — no root needed — yields a `.ab` archive containing the user's profile database in the clear. On iOS, apps that store PII in an unencrypted plist without the appropriate Data Protection class have had that data pulled straight out of an unencrypted iTunes backup. Forensic and law-enforcement tooling is built precisely around harvesting app data from device backups, and engagements routinely surface names, emails, tokens, and even ID-document scans sitting unencrypted in `shared_prefs` or a SQLite file. The consequence is mass PII exposure from a single backup, not a live exploit.
stepsToIdentify: Decompile the APK and check `AndroidManifest.xml` for `android:allowBackup` (true or unset on older targets) and the presence/contents of any `fullBackupContent`/`dataExtractionRules` XML that should exclude sensitive files.

Populate a test account with representative PII, exercise the app, then enumerate the app's data directory (`/data/data/<pkg>/` on a rooted device or emulator) and grep files for the known PII values in cleartext.
On Android with `allowBackup` enabled, run `adb backup` for the package, unpack the archive, and confirm which PII-bearing files are captured in the backup.

On iOS, create a local unencrypted backup and browse it (or inspect the app container on a jailbroken device) for plists/SQLite/JSON files containing PII, and check whether files use an appropriate Data Protection class.
Inspect SharedPreferences/plist/SQLite contents specifically for high-sensitivity fields (auth tokens, DOB, government ID, address, location history) stored without encryption.

Determine whether any at-rest encryption exists and, if so, whether the key is derived from user authentication or is a static/hardcoded key retrievable from the app (which is no better than plaintext).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes local-storage extraction and backup analysis against the test installation and test account.
Seed the test account with identifiable PII and use the app so the data is written locally.
Extract the app's stored data via the lowest-privilege path that works — `adb backup` for a backup-enabled app, otherwise filesystem read on a rooted/jailbroken device or emulator.
Locate the PII in the extracted files and demonstrate that it is readable in cleartext without the app's login being involved.
If the app claims encryption, show the data is either unencrypted or protected by a key recoverable from the binary/device, so the protection is ineffective.
Document each PII field found, its storage location and format, the extraction path used (backup vs. device), and the manifest/entitlement flags that permitted backup capture.

examplePayloads.label: Check the backup flag and rules in the manifest
examplePayloads.command: apktool d target_app.apk -o out && grep -iE 'allowBackup|fullBackupContent|dataExtractionRules' out/AndroidManifest.xml

examplePayloads.label: Extract app data via adb backup (Android, allowBackup=true)
examplePayloads.command: adb backup -f app.ab -noapk com.target.app && dd if=app.ab bs=1 skip=24 | openssl zlib -d > app.tar 2>/dev/null; tar xvf app.tar

examplePayloads.label: Grep the app data directory for PII in cleartext (rooted/emulator)
examplePayloads.command: adb shell run-as com.target.app grep -rniE 'email|phone|dob|aadhaar|passport|@example.test' shared_prefs/ databases/ files/

examplePayloads.label: Inspect a SharedPreferences / plist file for stored PII
examplePayloads.command: adb shell run-as com.target.app cat shared_prefs/user_profile.xml   # iOS: plutil -p <backup>/AppDomain-com.target.app/Library/Preferences/com.target.app.plist

examplePayloads.label: Dump a local SQLite database for personal records
examplePayloads.command: adb shell run-as com.target.app sqlite3 databases/app.db '.tables' && adb shell run-as com.target.app sqlite3 databases/app.db 'SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 5;'

variants: `android:allowBackup="true"` allows `adb backup` extraction of the full app data set over USB with no root required.
iOS PII stored in an unencrypted plist/SQLite without a Data Protection class, extractable from an unencrypted iTunes/Finder backup.
Data 'encrypted' with a hardcoded or app-derivable static key, so the ciphertext is trivially decryptable once the file is obtained.
Sensitive files written to shared/external storage or a cache that is world-readable or captured by cloud backup, exposing PII to other apps and to the cloud.
mitigation: Set `android:allowBackup="false"` for sensitive apps, or use precise `dataExtractionRules`/`fullBackupContent` to exclude every file containing PII or secrets from both cloud and device-to-device backups.
Encrypt PII at rest with keys held in the Android Keystore / iOS Keychain-Secure Enclave, bound to user authentication where appropriate, never with a static or hardcoded key.
On iOS, apply an appropriate Data Protection class (e.g. NSFileProtectionComplete) and mark files not needing backup with the do-not-back-up attribute; store secrets in the Keychain, not plists.
Data-minimize local persistence: store only what the app must cache, avoid keeping government IDs / full profiles on device, and purge sensitive caches on logout.
Use platform secure-storage abstractions (Android EncryptedSharedPreferences/Jetpack Security, iOS Keychain) rather than plaintext SharedPreferences/plists for any sensitive value.
Verify at-rest protection as a release gate by attempting a backup/filesystem extraction of a seeded test account and confirming no PII is recoverable in cleartext.
MOBILE-043.mitigationClientFacing: Your app saves users' personal information on the device in plain, readable form and does not stop it from being copied into device backups. That means the data can be pulled out of a backup on a computer or in the cloud, or read directly off a lost or stolen phone, without anyone ever logging into the app. In other words, all of your app's own protections are bypassed the moment the data leaves through a backup. The fix is to encrypt sensitive information on the device using the phone's secure hardware, to keep it out of backups, and to store as little of it locally as possible. This matters because the data at risk is exactly the personal information users trust you to keep safe.

MOBILE-044.prerequisites: The target application installed on a test device or emulator with a test account. Filesystem access to the app's snapshot/cache directory (rooted/jailbroken device or emulator recommended). The ability to background the app and open the OS task switcher/app-switcher. Authorization to inspect on-device cached images and screenshots.
MOBILE-044.whatItIs: When the user backgrounds the app, both Android and iOS take a screenshot of the current screen to show a preview in the recent-apps/task switcher, and they save that image to disk. If a sensitive screen — account details, a statement, an OTP, a scanned ID, personal messages — is on display, the OS caches a picture of that PII. The same happens where the app itself writes screenshots or lets sensitive screens be captured, leaving personal data in image files any process or person with device access can read.
MOBILE-044.rootCause: The task-switcher snapshot is a platform convenience the OS performs automatically, and apps must explicitly opt out of it (FLAG_SECURE on Android, or obscuring the UI on `applicationDidEnterBackground` on iOS). Developers focus on the app's own storage and network and overlook that the OS is caching a rendered image of whatever is on screen. Combined with not marking sensitive activities as secure and not blocking manual screenshots, this leaves rendered PII sitting in the snapshot cache.
MOBILE-044.impact: The cached snapshot preserves whatever PII was on screen — balances, personal identifiers, one-time codes, message content — in an image file that survives after the app is closed and is readable via device access, another app with storage permission, a backup, or forensic tooling. On a shared, lost, or stolen device the previews can reveal sensitive information without unlocking the app, and where the app permits screenshots of sensitive flows, users or malware can capture and exfiltrate that PII as images.
MOBILE-044.realWorldContext: The task-switcher snapshot leak is a staple of mobile banking and healthcare assessments and has driven concrete guidance: OWASP MASVS explicitly requires that sensitive screens are not exposed via the app-switcher, and banking apps that failed to set FLAG_SECURE have been flagged in audits for caching account balances into the recents preview. The recognizable finding is backgrounding an app on the account-summary or OTP screen and then pulling the cached PNG from the app's snapshot directory to reveal the balance or code in clear image form. On iOS the equivalent is a snapshot of the sensitive view written to the app's `Library/Caches/Snapshots` (or `SplashBoard`) directory. The impact is real-world shoulder-surfing-at-scale plus recoverable image evidence of PII on the device.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the app's sensitive screens (account/profile details, statements, OTP entry, ID capture, private messages) and log in with a test account so representative PII is displayed.
Display a sensitive screen, background the app (Home), and open the task switcher — observe whether the preview shows the real PII or a masked/blank placeholder.

On a rooted/jailbroken device or emulator, locate the OS snapshot cache and pull the most recent image, confirming whether it contains the sensitive screen's PII (Android: app snapshot cache; iOS: `Library/Caches/Snapshots`/`SplashBoard`).
Attempt a manual screenshot on each sensitive screen to determine whether screen capture is blocked (Android FLAG_SECURE) or permitted, and check for screen-recording exposure.

Review decompiled code for `WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE` usage (Android) or an `applicationDidEnterBackground` overlay/`isProtectedDataAvailable` handling (iOS) to see whether sensitive screens are protected.
Check any app-generated image caches (e.g. cached ID-document scans, downloaded statement thumbnails) for PII stored as images beyond the OS snapshot.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes on-device cache inspection and screenshot testing against the test installation and test account.
Log in and navigate to a sensitive PII screen, then background the app to trigger the OS snapshot.
Retrieve the cached snapshot image from the app's snapshot/cache directory and open it to show the PII is preserved in cleartext image form.
Demonstrate the task-switcher preview itself rendering the sensitive data to anyone with brief device access.
Where manual screenshots are allowed on sensitive screens, capture one to show the app does not prevent user/malware capture of PII.
Document each sensitive screen affected, the cached image location and its PII contents, and whether screenshots/recording were preventable but not prevented.

Manual screenshots and screen recording permitted on sensitive screens, letting the user or on-device malware capture PII as images.
App-generated image caches (cached statement thumbnails, retained ID-document scans) storing PII as picture files beyond the OS snapshot.
Snapshot of a screen showing a one-time passcode or transaction confirmation cached to disk, exposing a transient secret after it should have gone.
mitigation: Apply `FLAG_SECURE` to every activity that renders sensitive data on Android, which both blocks screenshots/recording and prevents the screen appearing in the recents snapshot.
On iOS, obscure sensitive content when entering the background (install a blank/blur overlay in `applicationDidEnterBackground`/`sceneWillResignActive`) so the cached snapshot contains no PII.
Do not display more sensitive data on screen than necessary, and mask high-sensitivity fields (full account numbers, OTPs, ID numbers) by default with reveal-on-demand.
Avoid persisting rendered PII as images in app caches; purge any sensitive image caches (ID scans, statement thumbnails) promptly and store them encrypted while retained.
Prevent screen recording where the platform allows (Android detect/secure, iOS `UIScreen.isCaptured` handling) for the most sensitive flows.
Add a task-switcher and screenshot check to the release/QA process for each sensitive screen so a regression that re-exposes PII in the snapshot is caught before shipping.
MOBILE-044.mitigationClientFacing: When a user switches away from your app, the phone automatically takes a picture of whatever is on screen to show a thumbnail in the recent-apps view, and it saves that picture on the device. If a screen showing personal information — an account balance, a one-time code, an ID scan — is visible at that moment, that personal data is captured into an image that stays on the device and can be recovered later or simply seen by anyone glancing at the recent-apps list. The fix is to tell the phone to protect your sensitive screens so they are hidden in that preview and cannot be screenshotted, and to hide sensitive content the instant the app goes to the background. This closes an easy way for personal data to leak from a shared, lost, or stolen phone.

The fix is to require encryption, trust only the system's built-in certificates, and remove any relaxed settings left over from testing. MOBILE-054.prerequisites: The APK/IPA and analysis tools (jadx, apktool), a test device. Authorization to reverse-engineer.
MOBILE-054.whatItIs: Apps that encrypt local data must protect the encryption key. If the key is hardcoded in the binary, derived from a predictable value, or stored insecurely, an attacker can recover it and decrypt the protected data. This tests for weak or hardcoded encryption keys.
MOBILE-054.rootCause: Developers hardcode or trivially-derive keys for simplicity, and because the app runs on a controlled device, the key is recoverable — defeating the encryption entirely.
MOBILE-054.impact: A recovered key lets an attacker decrypt all data the app 'protected', exposing credentials, tokens, and sensitive local data — making the encryption effectively useless.
MOBILE-054.realWorldContext: Hardcoded and predictably-derived encryption keys are a common mobile crypto failure: the data is encrypted, but the key is right there in the binary. Deriving keys from user secrets and storing them in the platform keystore is what makes local encryption meaningful.

The fix is to store encryption keys in the phone's secure hardware-backed keystore, derive them from user secrets where appropriate, and never build keys into the app.

MOBILE-055.impact: Weak algorithms let an attacker break encryption, forge hashes, or bypass integrity checks, defeating the protection the crypto was meant to provide (data confidentiality, integrity, authentication).
MOBILE-055.realWorldContext: Weak-crypto findings — MD5 for passwords, ECB-mode encryption revealing patterns, home-grown ciphers — are staples of mobile assessments. Using vetted, strong algorithms with correct modes is basic crypto hygiene that weak choices repeatedly violate.

MOBILE-056.realWorldContext: Insecure randomness for tokens and session IDs has enabled session hijacking and token prediction in real apps. Using a cryptographically secure RNG (SecureRandom) for all security-sensitive values is the fix, and using the default RNG for them is a recurring mistake.

MOBILE-057.prerequisites: The APK/IPA, a test device, and analysis tools. Authorization to test.
MOBILE-057.whatItIs: Encrypting data provides confidentiality but not integrity: if an app uses unauthenticated encryption (e.g. AES-CBC without a MAC), an attacker who can modify the ciphertext may tamper with the decrypted data undetected, potentially via padding-oracle or bit-flipping attacks. This tests for missing integrity protection on encrypted data.
MOBILE-057.rootCause: Developers use encryption modes that provide confidentiality only (CBC/CTR without a MAC) and assume encryption implies integrity, leaving ciphertext malleable.
MOBILE-057.impact: Without integrity protection, an attacker can tamper with encrypted data (bit-flipping, padding-oracle) to alter decrypted values or extract plaintext, undermining the data's trustworthiness and sometimes confidentiality.
MOBILE-057.realWorldContext: Missing integrity on encrypted data enables padding-oracle and bit-flipping attacks that have broken real systems. Using authenticated encryption (AES-GCM or encrypt-then-MAC) is the fix, and unauthenticated CBC without a MAC is a recurring weakness.

Assess whether ciphertext can be modified and still decrypt (no integrity check).

Assess the tampering/plaintext-recovery impact.
Document the missing-integrity weakness.

Determine whether integrity (MAC/AEAD) is applied.
Attempt controlled ciphertext modification and observe whether it is detected.

Document the integrity gap.

MOBILE-057.mitigationClientFacing: Encrypting data keeps it secret but doesn't stop someone from tampering with it unless you also add an integrity check. Without one, an attacker can alter the encrypted data in ways that change the result when it's decrypted. The fix is to use encryption that also verifies integrity (authenticated encryption) and to reject any data whose integrity check fails. This ensures encrypted data cannot be silently altered without detection, closing a gap that encryption alone does not cover.

MOBILE-058.whatItIs: Apps use biometrics (fingerprint/face) to gate access, but if the biometric result is checked in the app without being cryptographically bound to a keystore operation, an attacker can hook the callback to force a success. This tests whether biometric authentication is implemented securely or can be bypassed by runtime manipulation.

MOBILE-058.impact: Bypassing biometric authentication grants access to protected functionality/data without the biometric, defeating the control — especially impactful where biometrics gate sensitive features or data.
MOBILE-058.realWorldContext: Biometric-bypass via Frida hooking the success callback is a standard mobile test, and apps that use the event-bound biometric API rather than binding a keystore key to the biometric are routinely defeated. Crypto-bound biometrics (a key released only on success) is the secure pattern.
